utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. May we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. It's always difficult, a situation for Trial Chamber when the Trial Chamber knows that the accused has, or in this case had had -- has had birthday, and as we just learned, today it is his sacred patron saint today. Dr. Stakic, please understand that it's difficult because it may sound cynical to wish you a happy birthday. All what we can wish you is all the best, and may you find justice, fair representatives here in the Court, and hopefully a fair Trial Chamber. So all the best for you. We are confronted with a request by the Defence to abbreviate today's session. On the other hand, we were confronted by the request by the OTP to have a shorter session tomorrow. In principle, we always have to live with our schedule. And therefore, there's no leeway to abbreviate on purpose without due cause. I think it's absolutely necessary that Dr. Stakic has the possibility to meet the Defence team today in order to prepare for tomorrow. So therefore, I would ask you to contact Detention Unit; if there are any impediments related to the time, please let me know that I can take the necessary measures. I have to tell you that tomorrow's witness wishes all protective measures possible. Therefore, I should like to hear your comments on all the three issues I just mentioned, very briefly, please. First, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We never object to any kind of protective measures to anybody -- for anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. And you, please, let me -- let us know in case there should be difficulties with the visiting hours today. Let's see how long the witness will take us. But in principle, the Defence should be prepared to call a second witness also today. And what about the Prosecution? Any submissions as regards the protective measures and the hearing dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. But we anticipate this witness will not be that short, and if we do start a second witness, that witness will have to be interrupted for the following Court-scheduled witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's try to decide spontaneously on the basis what happens today. A last formal announcement of a decision: This Trial Chamber was seized with the question whether or not to take action under Rule 91 related to Witness Dragic, whether or not there should be a direction to the Prosecutor to investigate the matter. The Trial Chamber found that it would be premature to decide at this point in time whether or whether not to take these measures before we have the entire evidence before us. With a view to the entire evidence, we may come to a different result, and therefore, we will not decide on this before the end of the case. I can't see any obstacles for hearing now today's witness. We received an amended proffer. Another indication that the work load for all participants is too high, meeting even on Sunday when entering or leaving the tram. I think there should be some restrictions as regards the workload. So, as usual, the question, any new protective measures to be requested for the following witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No protective measures for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then ask the usher to escort the witness Milos Jankovic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jankovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I can, sure. Shall I say my name? Will this be interpreted? Yes, yes, excellent. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You testified earlier before this Tribunal in May 2001. You are a little bit acquainted with the procedure. May I therefore ask you to give us now your solemn declaration in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. And the witness is for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. John Ostojic I represent, as you know, Mr. Stakic before this Tribunal. Will you be so kind as to state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milos Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is your father's name?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: My father's name is Jovo, and my mother's name is Petra.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of October, 1948, in the village of Gornji Zabar, later it was re-named Pelagicevo. The municipality used to be Gradacac, but now Pelagicevo belongs to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not that I'm unhappy with your answer, I'm just waiting for the interpretation to finish. So I would like to ask you to, after my question, to please pause for a while and watch on the screen when the interpretation is over. Where do you live today?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: My permanent place of residence is Prijedor. I have my own flat there. I bought it off my company. The street is Metropolita Petra Zimonjica. The building is C3 and flat number 23. I work in Banja Luka, so throughout the working week, I often spent my nights in Banja Luka and stay with people I know, but my official address is in Prijedor, the one I've just given you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us your occupation and what sort of school you finished.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in electronics and telecommunications. I completed secondary school for mechanical engineering, elementary school in my own village, and then secondary school for mechanical engineering in Brcko. And then later on, I went to study at the electronics faculty in Banja Luka. After that, my occupation has been a degree in electronics and telecommunication. I'm an engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where do you work today?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: At the public security centre in Banja Luka, department for communications. The official name is Communications Department. I am the head of a group for maintenance of all communications equipment. There are five or six technicians in the team. I lead the team. And I'm in charge of maintenance and mounting the equipment, if necessary. It's the technical part of the job for all communications, telecommunications equipment used by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you work in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I started working for the police in 1980, until the last year, I kept working for the police, and I was also employed by the police in 1992 in Prijedor. It was called Public Security Station Prijedor. I was also head of that same department for telecommunications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you the following: Were you ever a member of any political party, or are you today a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the socialist system in the former Yugoslavia, it was almost a requirement to be a member of the League of Communists. And in view of the position I held, I virtually had to be a member. Afterwards, when the League of Communists disintegrated, and the multiparty system was in place, I was never again a member of any political party. I didn't belong to any political party, nor was I in the least involved with any of the political parties. I just wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain the following: In 1992, what were your duties as head of the communications department and cryptographic protection?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Ever since I worked in that job, I've had the same duties, and I had the same duties then: I must be familiar with the way the department is organised, its activities, the activities of the police; and my job was to adjust and organise all communications, people working for communications; organise all the equipment in order to secure an efficient transfer of information. We are talking about written information, we are talking about telegrams, dispatches, as well as oral communication, communication by telephone, radio; the sort of communication used by the police. I was in charge of organising and enhancing the quality of the communications service. Nothing else. This also implied working with information that needed to be encoded, protected cryptographically, so protection of information was also part of my business, and I'm talking about such information as needed protecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I will show you a table. So if you could please comment on it. It's written in English, but I think we'll manage to deal with it nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could the usher please show the witness this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear anything and I can't really see it here. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you managed to have a look?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just have a minute to look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If it would be helpful, I do have a B/C/S copy of that same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Am I correct that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I can understand this, what it says here, even without the translation. This is fine. So if there's no need for you to have the original, I don't really need one. I understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I, nevertheless, interrupt for a moment. Is there any B/C/S version, or is this a document provided later on? Because the addition of the ethnicity to the persons mentioned there seems to be a little bit strange. But I don't know. What is the source of this document? Can you comment already on this now, or do you want to come back to this later?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received this document from the Prosecution, and this is obvious, if you look at the number on this document. So this document is part of the testimony given by one of the commanders of the police station in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to come back to this issue later. There are no definite objections by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, if you look at this diagram, can you please explain to us the chain of command in your own public security station at that time, starting with the Sarajevo MUP.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I've had a look in the meantime, and I think there are several mistakes here. I'm going to start with the MUP and try to explain, because I think I can still remember exactly how it was at that time. I'm going to try to insert the corrections. The police, the hierarchy of the police, we were all directly or indirectly subordinated to the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It says here: "MUP Sarajevo, Minister Delimustafic." That was correct at the time. And then Avdo Hebib, as far as I know, this MUP box here, it had two different sectors, public and state security. I, as well as all the other police, was public security, and state security was a different sector. We were often in the same building, but state security answered to their own boss in MUP. But certainly, they were indirectly subordinated. The uppermost box I'm pointing at, the MUP, only this line here should really be there, and then it says, "Banja Luka security centre, Stojan Zupljanin." That's correct. But what isn't correct is there are other centres here, like Doboj, Zenica. But certainly you can't only have SUP Prijedor here because the Prijedor SUP, this line here leading to the Prijedor SUP, should go into this other box, State Security Section Banja Luka, and not the one above. The Prijedor SUP, that was not an official name at the time. It wasn't its official name. This was from the socialist system. It was the Secretariat for Internal Affairs. You see, it's different. Up there it says MUP, and down here it says SUP. There is the Ministry of the Interior, and this is not a SUP. This should be SJB Prijedor. That would be the correct way to spell it, the public security station. But I know what this is referring to. It's true, there was Hasan Talundzic at the time, and he was a Muslim. This section here, State Security Service, and their sector was directly subordinated to the central office, although it was in the same building in Prijedor, but that means the connection is not this but straight up and then through them, on to the MUP. If you can see what I'm trying to explain. The Banja Luka centre, in addition to the SUP, there were other security agencies; Dubica, Gradiska, so in other words, other municipalities. And the police across those municipalities, they were called the SJB, public security stations. And now I will tell you about the Prijedor public security station. The public security station in Prijedor had a number of organisation units. Here -- this was normally considered the main one, the police down here, what you can see. And they were wearing uniforms, and they were officials. So they were considered to be the main office. And then you have something down here, too, but that doesn't matter because they were really the most important part of the station and of any station. And then beside them, it says crime, but the official title was Crime Prevention Unit, Fire Prevention and Foreigners. That was the full name, but it's true that Ranko Mijic was the head, and that he was a Serb. Then there was a small subsection, communications. We were also officials of the public security station. There were usually between five and seven of us, and you see my name here. I was the head of that particular section, and that's also true. And then this part here, general affairs, I think that's what it says, Slavica. The official name, the one we used, was Section for General and Administrative Affairs. They were in charge of citizens' IDs, driving licenses. They would issue citizens with passports. For the needs of the citizens, for the needs of the public, they were in charge of that. It says Slavica, yes, that's right. Her last name was Manojlovic, at this time as far as I can remember. There were changes, frequent changes, I'm also sure that she was the head at the time, but they had new heads of department all the time, quite frequently. Now I'm talking about the police division. So it says Prijedor Station, Dusan Jankovic, Serb. This was the general police station, and we had the traffic police. The name was "milicija" at that time; now we refer to it as "policija," so I'll just stick to "policija." We have Prijedor station. Their commander was Dusan Jankovic. And that's correct. And then here it says Omarska station, Milutin Bujic. There is a mistake here. Omarska station was not a station that was part of a formation at that time. Not at that time. It used to be once upon a time, but at this time it was only a branch office, it was a department. So commander did not have a deputy. And they didn't have as many people working there. That's to the best of my recollection. I think I'm not wrong on this one, but it was a long time ago. Milutin Bujic, partly yes, he was removed at one point, but I can't remember when exactly. Here it says Kozarac station. This is not correct. Kozarac was also just a department. The commander was Osman Didovic, a Muslim, that is also correct. And he had no deputy because this was only a police department, not a station. Ljubija station. Now, Ljubija was a station. And Branko Bjekic, a Croat, was its commander. I can't remember who his deputy was during this period. If someone reminded me, perhaps I would remember, but right now I can't seem to recall who the deputy was. Traffic. Fikret Kadiric. This was called Traffic Safety Police Station. So those were traffic police. They were in charge of controlling traffic along the roads and ensuring the safety of traffic. We're talking about cars and personal vehicles, not about trains. He was a Muslim. Yes, that's correct. This was also a police station, like all the other stations. It had its commander. They would control and monitor traffic along public roads, so that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, Mr. Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, may I just interrupt. For technical reasons, may we have a break of about 3 minutes. Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.37 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please continue. Thank you. May I only ask, do we know about this document from what point or what point in time this document reflects?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who is supposed to answer; me or you. Is it me who is supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Every question is put to you. I cannot testify.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Given the names, as far as I can remember, Minister Delimustafic, SUP Prijedor; Hasan Talundzic, this must be the period after the multiparty elections. Because this is when they were appointed, after that, and after the end -- after the takeover, after that, Hasan Talundzic and Delimustafic were not any longer, after the 30th of April, 1992. It is certain that this is the period from their appointment. As far as I can remember, it was in the spring of 1991. I can't give you the precise date. But between the spring of 1991 until the spring, or more precise, April 1992. The one who put together this table, I don't know what period he meant when he put the table together, but this must be that period because at that time, we were the public security station, and not a centre. We were the public security station, and we didn't have -- there was a restriction in our organisation. So what I said, Omarska and Kozarac were not stations; they were departments or subsections. That implies fewer people, and that is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this chain of command and reporting and giving orders, can there be a municipal body? Can a municipal body appear, a body of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor? Can it appear in this chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously it is not here. And whoever put the table together knew that there wasn't. I know that there wasn't. We are police, and like the army, we have our hierarchy of command. And I was just a small -- head of a small department, and my boss was the chief of the public security station. At this period of time, it was Hasan Talundzic. Previously there were other people, later on there were other people. Hasan Talundzic, he should have been -- there is a mistake here in the drawing. This line is wrong. This line is correct. So Hasan Talundzic's boss was the chief of the public security centre in Banja Luka, Stojan Zupljanin, and he, Stojan Zupljanin, reported to the minister in Sarajevo, the Minister of the Interior in Sarajevo. So this is the hierarchy. This is the chain of command. If people obey it or not is a different story, but this is the rule here. In my work, I knew whom I was supposed to obey; that was my head. And he had to obey his head, and he had to obey the minister, and the minister had to report to the government, and that is the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before April 1992, was the situation the same? And after the September of 1992, was the situation again the same as it was between the April and September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not referring to the names; I'm referring to the police, whether in all the periods -- can you please listen to my question, sir. Was there a rule in place in all the periods of time that the bodies of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor could not interfere with the work of the police in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the first period. What was the first period that you mentioned? What period of time are you referring to, the first period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1991 and onwards, was it ever the case that a body of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, that they could order something to you as the head of the department?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they couldn't issue any orders as far as I can remember. But there were influences outside the police, and that is that the parties proposed heads of departments. But it was the minister who appointed them. For example, the chief of the public security station and the commander. But the parties, as far as I can remember, as far as I was informed - I was not in the position to know that, it was not my obligation to know that - but I was familiar with something, but some things were arranged at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was that the chief of the police was appointed by the ruling party in the municipality, and in Prijedor it was the SDA. And they appointed Hasan Talundzic. And the second, by the number of votes, was the SDS, and they were supposed to appoint the commander. Not appoint, but they proposed the commander and the minister was the one that the commander would go for talks in Sarajevo, and the minister would then issue a decision, and the minister would then appoint this person, and that was, at the time, Dusan Jankovic. So that is that. Everything else was done beyond the influence of the parties. And I'm not aware of the fact that the Municipal Assembly had any influence, and I don't know what would be the basis of their influence. I don't think it is under the law. As far as I was concerned, I had my head, and he had his head, and the municipality was something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally ever receive from the municipality of Prijedor or its Executive Board any orders from them? Did you receive any orders from them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. There were at the time people who were not experienced, who were not knowledgeable, and even they were clear that they couldn't issue such orders. The only orders I could receive and obey were from my commanders, from my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the time being, we will not need the document that is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, should this document be marked provisionally as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it's your intention to tender it, we can immediately decide. Any objections by the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then may I ask the next exhibit number for Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D46A, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, D46A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the takeover in Prijedor, what happened with the transmitter on Kozara? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: A transmitter on Kozara carried the programmes on two channels. There were two channels of Sarajevo TV. And I don't remember when it was, but I believe it was at the beginning of 1991 that that transmitter on Kozara -- I won't claim that for a fact. I believe that one channel was adjusted to carry programmes from TV Belgrade. I can't claim this for a fact, but I believe that one of the channels was still dedicated for TV Sarajevo, and the other one was adjusted for TV Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did that happen? Why was the transmitter adjusted to receive Belgrade, programmes from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Those who do that, the technicians and all those who make decisions and technicians who are supposed to carry out the decisions, they are all in Banja Luka because television Sarajevo had in Banja Luka a branch office so to say, and they were the ones who were deciding on the policies, on the programmes, on the transmitters. And for us in Prijedor, the only thing that happened was that shows were different, programmes were different. Some people liked it. Some not. I don't watch television much, but I noticed that -- this change, that that was that. I was not very much interested in what had happened, but I don't know if anybody from Prijedor had any influence on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us whether you could also receive Croatian programmes after the transmitter was adjusted to receive programmes from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I am an expert in electrical engineering, I can tell you that in the area of the town of Prijedor, my acquaintances very often will ask me for help when they want to receive some programmes from Zagreb. And since I'm an expert on that, and this is my particular field of interest, I can tell you with a high degree of expertise, I am familiar with the situation. The town of Prijedor and its general area belong, in rough outlines, to the area covered by the transmitters of Croatian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the Croatian television which -- where are they based?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: They are based all over Croatia, and the most powerful one is on the mountain Pljesivica, above Bihac. That facility is on the border. I don't know exactly where, but it is on the border between the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. It is the mountain of Pljesivica above Bihac. There are some other transmitters. There are the ones that are closer in the north of Croatia, but they are limited in their outreach by the Kozara mountain. And because of what I have just said, citizens of Prijedor, some of them could receive programmes from Croatia. They had the picture, they had the turn. Maybe not of the highest possible quality, but they could receive it. And there were, on the other hand, some other citizens who couldn't receive those programmes. And those areas, due to the laws of physics, all of these areas are very close. So, for example, I have a case of my friend, a Croat. He asked me to help him receive a programme from Zagreb, but I couldn't do it, whereas his neighbour, whose house is only 60 metres away across the road, could receive it. I tried to help the former one, but I couldn't. So some people could receive these programmes; others couldn't. And it all depended on where their TV receiver was actually placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the situation the same during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was. There are such areas, because this is an uneven ground. For example, I can give you an example of my in-laws' house. Their antennas are in such a position that they could not receive the programmes from Kozara, which is only 5 or 6 kilometres away. And they could receive programmes from Zagreb, which is hundreds of kilometres away, because there is a different optical visibility to Pljesivica, and between them and Kozara, there was another very high hill. So there are even such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to move from these technical issues to the 9th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the usher to show you a document. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain what this is about, and do you still have the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I start?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a photocopy of a paper whose original I still have to this very day. Why have I kept such papers? This may be due to my occupation. I collect all the papers and then I discard some, because there are many papers at my home which are not important. This is one of those papers which I have kept. The day, the 9th of April, I couldn't remember the date. I know that this is certainly the 9th of April, because this is my handwriting, and I can remember this very well. And this is what it was all about. On the 9th of April, I had to maintain some facilities in Novi Grad, which was then called Bosanski Novi. And I went there with one of my technicians, and we repaired some facilities there. And around 2.00, we returned to Prijedor, to the public security station. And I had only heard before that, and I didn't find that important, but I heard it, and I remembered it, that the chief of the public security centre in Banja Luka, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, was supposed to come to the municipality of Prijedor, and that he was supposed to negotiate or agree on the -- I believe actually we belong, this public security station belonged to the central public security centre in Banja Luka, and there were some intentions to separate us from the centre. And this is what I assume. Nobody actually told me. Nobody had to tell me. I didn't ask anybody. But that's what I felt, because that was a topical issue at the time. And I suppose that's why he came there to talk to the municipal bodies. I don't mean municipal, but that's what also was always said. These authorities, those authorities, he was supposed to talk to Mirza Mujadzic and people around him. And Mirza Mujadzic was the head of the SDA for Prijedor, so he had to talk to the parties. That was my conclusion. And I cannot be certain about that. And it wasn't important at the time. But that's what I heard, that he was supposed to arrive there. And what I deemed important at the time was that he was my superior, and I didn't want him to notice that anything was not in order. And that's what I was concerned with. But as I said, I went to Novi Grad, I had some facilities to maintain there, and then we came back. The technician, whose name was Mladen Raus, and myself, we returned at 2.00. Working hours were until 3.00. It was 1400 hours, and my working hours were until 1500 hours. When we got in front of the SUP building, and when we drove the car into the courtyard and parked it there, we approached the SUP building -- that's what I refer to this building as although it was the public security station -- I noticed in the whole area, as far as I could see around the building of the public security station, the municipal building in front of the park, as far as I could see up to the park and around it, I saw very many groups of younger people with -- wearing jackets with their hands in their pockets. And each group consisted of between three and five people, and there were some ten -- they were some 10 or 20 metres from each other. And the distances between them were not the same. I entered the SJB building, and the communications centre where I worked is on the top of the building. There is the ground floor, the first floor, and the second floor. I am on the second floor, at the end of the corridor, together with the rest of my department, the rest of my section. When I entered the building, there were exceptionally few people moving around the corridors. Usually there are citizens, there are employees of the public security station. There was nobody there. I approached the door of my department, which is always locked, and the only ones who are allowed to enter are the employees of that particular department. On the right-hand side, some metre, 1 metre from my door, there's the door of the office where Mr. Muharem Seric worked. As far as I can remember, at the time he was the official in charge of the reserve police, which was then called milicija. And I could see his door opening, and three or four people coming out of the office, middle-aged people, very quiet, leaving the office in a single file. One of them was a bit older, maybe my age, and he told the others: "Okay, single file, just slowly." To my mind, that was a very unusual scene, almost unrealistic. Something was obviously not right there. I entered my office and then I approached the window, and I could see through the window that there were a lot of people there. I couldn't see any noise, but I could see them talking. And those that I had just seen coming out of that office, the four or five people that I had just seen, I now saw them leaving our building, and each of them approaching a different group, telling them something, and then moving on. I found that very suspicious. And then in the same corridor on the same floor, on the other side of the corridor, there was my wife's office. She worked in the crime police at the time. And the official title of that department was the Crime Prevention Department, as I've already said. So I went there, and I asked her what this was all about. She didn't know. That's the kind of person that she is; she doesn't have a clue, she just does her job. She doesn't notice anything, and she didn't notice anything on that day. Then I asked her to leave her office then and walk with me. I was concerned. Why was I concerned? Because there were tensions, and the tensions increased. I hoped that they would diminish, but they kept on increasing. That's why I asked her to leave her office and to walk with me in front of the SUP building. And that's what we did. We passed by -- in front of the municipal building. We walked around the park. We made a circle around that area and a circle in the diameter of some hundred metres. And in rough outlines -- I didn't count them precisely, but I could tell that there were some 50 or 60 groups of people in that large area in that huge park in front of the museum, in front of the mine, in front of the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please make your explanation a bit shorter, and can we come to that meeting when Zupljanin arrived in the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. So according to my estimate, there were perhaps about 300 people in that huge area, assembling in groups. When I returned, I went to see the secretary. She was the secretary of the -- of our chief, Hasan Talundzic. To the right of her, there was Ranko Mijic's office. He was chief of crime prevention. So I had a conversation with him. I asked him if he knew what was going on, and he didn't know either. And then the two of us were addressed by Mira, the chief's secretary. And she told us: "Don't go anywhere far. The chief said there would be a meeting in his office. We should call all the others to come to the meeting." That was in perhaps 20 minutes, she said; not too long, but not right away. So we came to the meeting. Actually, that's what I wrote down here. Stojan Zupljanin and together with him, his assistant for public security, Bajazit -- this is slightly illegible, but I think the man's last name was Jahic or Jehic. I think Jahic. He only held that position very briefly so I may not have memorised his name exactly. His first name was Bajazit, and his second name, I think, was Jahic. So there was supposed to be a meeting with them. We came in. Later I only heard in my conversations with other people that he could not have this meeting he was supposed to have at the municipality because Mirza Mujadzic, the president of the SDA, would not see him. And they were objecting about weapons. The driver did wear a uniform, and he did carry a weapon. Stojan Zupljanin and his assistant for public security were not armed -- were not wearing uniform. Whether they had weapons, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. Stojan Zupljanin's assistant, do you know what his name was and what his nationality was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: First name Bajazit. That much I'm sure of. I scribbled this down, so I'm not sure what the last name is. I think it's Jahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is his nationality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As the name itself says, he is a Muslim. And after the elections, there were Serbs and Muslims and Croats. This is a position within the internal organisation of the centre. You have the head, and then two assistants, one for public security and another for state security. So he has two assistants, two deputies. So Jahic was the assistant in charge of public security, so he was our superior before Zupljanin, who was like our top superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, who else attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I wrote it down here so it's clear for all to see. I was using abbreviations but I know who I was referring to. Here it says Stole -- those were nicknames that they used. "Stole" Stojan Zupljanin; "Hasan" Hasan Talundzic; "Dule" Dusan Jankovic, commander of our station; "Kecan" Radovan Kecan, assistant commander; "Ziko" Ziko was another assistant, another assistant commander. His name was Zijad Basic. "Fikret," Fikret was Fikret Kadiric, the commander of traffic police. "Djuro," I can't remember what he was at this time but he was a member of the police, too, Djuro Prpos. "Mijic," Ranko Mijic, chief of the crime squad. Myself, chief of communications and cryptographic protection. And then chief of public security, Bajazit Jahic. This is what I wrote down back then as I was in the meeting, when the meeting began.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was discussed at that meeting, if you could just provide a brief explanation, and why was that noteworthy?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, throughout that period, there were tendencies and one -- different tendencies, and one of the groups was striving, one of the many groups, because in terms of organisation, the public security station was part of the public security centre in Banja Luka. And then the public security centre was part of the MUP in Sarajevo. Some people strove to keep things this way, and other people wanted us to become an independent centre with equal rights as the Banja Luka centre. So they wanted us to split off from the Banja Luka centre. Those were supposed to be the municipalities that we had while we were the centre. Sometimes we were the centre, sometimes we weren't. I mean Prijedor. And now again, we weren't. So those four municipalities were supposed to split off; Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, and Prijedor. The seat was supposed to be the headquarters in Prijedor, and we were supposed to be directly subordinated to the MUP in Sarajevo, just like Banja Luka. So that was the idea. And both strove emphatically to achieve their aims, both groups, so we tried to reach a compromise, an agreement, to keep everyone happy. Now here, what I wrote, it's a bit difficult to read. It is my own handwriting. But it's slightly illegible. It says: "Stole said, for the JRM, Hasan tells me everything is as best as could be." JRM is short for units of the reserve police, units of the reserve police across the villages because every village had its own unit. And Stojan said that this was supposed to be our plan for preparations and how to secure the service. Hasan said our situation is smooth. Hasan is here speaking about the reserve forces. He wants weapons. Stole says this is militarisation. That's what I jotted down. These were just my own personal notes, not very accurate. But I know, and I remember on the basis of this, exactly what they spoke about. Hasan was saying, "We are well organised, sufficiently organised. Our personnel is very good, but we don't have enough weapons." I had attended several of those meetings before because I was part of this committee, so chiefs would meet, and I did hear them on several occasions talk about it. As far as I can remember, the reserve forces in Prijedor Municipality, we had 700 reserve police. And for the reserve forces, there were about 450 rifles, that means an insufficient amount of rifles. So Hasan was saying we need more weapons. And Stojan Zupljanin was saying, this is no good. If we focus all our activities on arming those people, then what we have on our hands is militarisation, he says. Then we practically take over the authority of the army, the functions of the army, and that's not our purpose. We're supposed to keep law and order in our own territory, and that's what we should focus on as opposed to providing weapons. The rifles that we have, I think, are enough for the work that needs to be done. That means Hasan wanted more weapons or turn the whole thing into an army. At least, that's what I heard at the meeting. So he wanted to focus on the military work and not on the police work. And now here it reads: "The transformation of the MUP, setting up of a CSB. Hasan and sometimes Fikret would join in the discussion, the commander, they were talking about the MUP being transformed. And what they meant was we, the Prijedor municipality with the three other municipalities I referred to, were not to be public security stations under Banja Luka, but that we ourselves should be an independent centre and directly to answer to the MUP in Sarajevo. So we would receive orders from the MUP in Sarajevo directly and this way they were channelled through Banja Luka. So here it says the transformation of the MUP, and he says I'm not in favour of carving the service up. That's what Stojan Zupljanin was saying, roughly. The point of his contribution was there's no need to carve the whole service up. This is not really essential to us. We, as the police, if we belong to the centre, we shall just look after our own work as the police. And then Hasan and Fikret don't want the badges. And then Fikret and Hasan replied to what he said, that they couldn't deal with Banja Luka, because in Banja Luka, certain policemen had started already - maybe all of them, I wasn't there at this time, but I know that something started happening. They began to -- because, you know, they were still wearing the five-star -- the five-point star insignia from socialism, which had gone out of use by that time. So by inertia, they were still using the same insignia as in the former Yugoslavia. And then in Banja Luka, they started using different insignia. They started wearing the badge that was in the form of a Serbian flag; red, blue, and white, a small beret with a badge on it. Hasan and Fikret, the commander, were saying that they couldn't agree to that, to wear Serb flags on their caps. And now here, I said that we should be unified and reach an agreement. I kept silent up to that point, but then I came forward and I said that first and foremost we needed to be united, to reach an agreement and to respect this agreement. We needed to be unified as the police. That's the way it used to be and that's the way it should stay. In the socialist system, we didn't look at people's ethnic backgrounds. We needed to say unified to alleviate the tensions and to try in every way to avert the danger of war and anything that was dangerous. So that's what I said. Let's reach an agreement and stick to that agreement. That was my contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, did Mr. Talundzic order the secretary not to let anyone into the meeting, and did she still let someone else into the meeting? Did she not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we entered the room in which the meeting was taking place, that was Talundzic's office, when we entered, the secretary stayed outside. Mira Topic, his secretary. He told her: "Mira, please, should anyone come calling, tell them I'm not here. Please don't interrupt us for anyone." And really, the discussion that I've recounted for you now, this may have lasted -- well, roughly speaking, it has been a long time -- one hour perhaps or a bit more. And then Mira came in at one point, and she said -- she spoke to Hasan, and she said: "Boss, Osme is looking for you." Osme was the only person with that name. She was speaking about Osme Didovic who was the commander of the Kozarac police department. Hasan stood up, left the room. He spoke to Osme. I didn't even see Osme, so they were speaking outside the office. He was back in a couple of minutes, but without Osme. He addressed us, and I could tell by just looking at his face that he was worried. He told us, "Well, look folks, things are getting really serious. There could be a war any moment now." And we asked, Well, what's the matter? And he said, Osme had come to tell him that. In Kozarac, their people now, whether they were mobilised or -- I'm talking about the police, but the police were not that many, maybe between 10 and 15 members of the police, I forgot exactly how many, but not too many, so their numerical strength was not great anyway. They were trying to raise a major number of people, and there was danger that they had head for Prijedor at any moment now. And there was word that they wanted to have their own government in Kozarac at that time. That sort of thing. And I said -- and then Hasan said, well, we must do something urgently to keep this from happening, to keep unrest from breaking out. And they decided very quickly to call, and within 10 to 15 minutes, they were there, two journalists. One was from the local paper, Kozarski Vjesnik, and the other journalist was from the local radio station, Radio Prijedor. I used to know one of them because we were neighbours. The journalist's name was Nezirevic. He was a Muslim. I can't remember his first name now. And the other journalist, I didn't know him at all, but I remember that he was a Serb because when we spoke to them, they were telling him he had a big head and curly hair. That's all I remember. But it was deliberately done that they invited two different journalists with two different ethnic backgrounds. And they told them about the situation, and they told them that they had to come up with some sort of announcement urgently in order to allay the tensions. The journalists got the idea very quickly, so they went back to their work. The meeting ended. I didn't listen to the radio and I didn't read the papers, but I did hear from my wife and from a number of neighbours that that was from 6.00 in the afternoon, the Radio Prijedor kept broadcasting this announcement for the people to stay calm, that the police had everything under control, that there would be no riot by any of the sides involved, any of the ethnic groups. They said everything was under control and they played soothing music to back their statements up. That's what I was told, that it was obvious that this was the case. So much for that particular meeting. I'm not sure if I've omitted anything of essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you. We forgot about the year. You said it was on 9th of April. Could you just tell us the year, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 9th of April, 1992. Here it reads, "9th of April, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, is it necessary to have this in the evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is tendered by you. I can't see any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be helpful to everyone if the witness would read it word for word for the record. Some of it he has read or interpreted. We don't really know what's written here, and even if we submit it for translation, they may have trouble with the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's a good idea. Could you please be so kind that we have access to that what you in fact had written at that time, the 9th of April, 1992, just to read consecutively what we can see on this piece of paper that shall be, then, D47B. And then we don't need any translation into English. It follows from today's pages 22 through 30 what is the content of the document. Could you please read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly. The date, the 9th of April. That's clear. "Chief of centre and the rest." That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please don't elucidate, just read what it says on the paper.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of centre and the rest. GL agreement. That means the main agreement. That's what I think it says. This is my personal shorthand. Present: Stole, Hasan, Dule, Kecan, Ziko, Fikret, Djuro -- you can't see it here but it should be here -- Mijic, myself, and chief of public security Bajazit Jahic. Please, I'm sure it's Jahic, so write "Jahic." Number 1, Stole said -- this is a Z, for JRM. This is unit of the reserve police. Comma, and Hasa, Hasan says that our situation is the best. Hasan speaks about reserve -- this refers to the reserve force, the reserve police force. That's what this means. Comma, he wants weapons. Stole -- that is Zupljanin -- Stole says this is militarisation. Number 2, this is item 2 on the agenda. Transformation of the MUP - setting up of the CSB. This is Item 2. Stole speaks about transformation of the MUP - I am not in favour of carving up the service. That's him speaking, not me. And here, dash, Hasan and Fikret don't want badges. This is nothing. This was just me scribbling and jotting down my own name and some lines. This arrow here, that means I was speaking myself. I spoke about specific agreement to stay unified. I meant all the workers, all the employees of the police, regardless of our ethnic backgrounds. That's that. This is my personal -- these are my personal notes, and this is the first time they are being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Once again, admitted into evidence, D47B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it be a convenient time, Your Honour, for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Lukic, if you want to continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like the usher to give the witness the document marked as D6, to give the witness the B/C/S version. Would you be so kind and turn the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's on purpose that we all should have the B/C/S version? I think we are improving, but not that good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or if the usher could put the English version on the ELMO, and present the witness with the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you've told us that in 1992, including the April of 1992, you worked in the Prijedor public security station.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When and on what date towards the end of April was a meeting organised in the building of the public security station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was organised. A meeting was organised. There was no written notification. There was no advance notice. As far as I knew, it was only a few hours before the meeting. I was not in the office on that day. I was somewhere making rounds, and when I came back, one of my employees told me about the meeting which was supposed to take place at 1400 hours, and that all the authorised personnel should be present at the meeting. I took that seriously. I informed all the other employees who reported to me in my department. I didn't even -- I didn't have the time to inform everybody, but most of them were there, and I was at that meeting myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the agenda known in advance?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I arrived at the meeting, I didn't know what the meeting was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you saw; who was chairing the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting was held in our conference room. When I say "our conference room," I mean the conference room of the public security station, where meetings are normally held. That is, the town hall meetings attended by all the employees. And the conference hall was full. All the chairs were occupied. Some of the people were even standing. Some people were even standing at the door, and they spilled over into the corridor. But they could listen what was going on in the conference room. There was the desk for the chairpersons. Maybe that is not the correct word to use, but those were the people who presided over the meeting. I wasn't sitting down. I was standing up, leaning on a column in the conference hall, so I was leaning against that column, and I was some 3 or 4 metres away from them. And these people were present from the left to the right, those people I had known already. I knew them already. So from the left, there was the president of the municipality, Cehajic. Muhamed or Muharem, I'm not sure about his first name. But I know him. He's an elderly man. His name is Cehajic, and he was the president of the municipality. And next to him was Mirza Mujadzic, the president of the SDA. In the middle -- there were five of them. In the middle, Hasan Talundzic, our chief of the station. Next to him, on his left, Fikret Kadiric, who was then the commander of the traffic police department, and then he was the chief of the police. And finally, Simo Miskovic. If I'm not mistaken, he was at the time the president of the SDS. So there were party members. A little bit further was the person who was taking the minutes, Radovan Kecan, the assistant commander of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anybody speak at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting was opened by Mr. Hasan Talundzic. And then there were other speakers. He spoke most of the time. But there were other individuals at the chair who took the floor. And in the latter part of the meeting, there was a debate, so those people who attended a meeting voiced their opinions, asked questions, and the people and the chairperson answered those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the debate about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: When the meeting was opened, it was said, but I can't quote the exact words, but it was clear, it transpired from those words that what was asked of the employees was the support of the police. And just like I said a little while ago, that we, as the public security station, would separate from the public security centre in Banja Luka and that we should join direct with Sarajevo. When I say "Sarajevo," I can't give you the details whether that was the Sarajevo MUP or maybe that we should be the centre, as we had been before, so that we could report directly to Sarajevo. And this was explained by the following: It was said that we would benefit from being directly subordinated to Sarajevo. Salaries did not arrive on time. We had already not received two salaries, and they told us that the salaries would arrive within one or two -- the first one would arrive within one or two days, and the second one would arrive a little after that. So people asked the floor. Some were in favour. Some were against. I can't really remember any of the names of those who asked the floor and who participated in the debate. So I can't tell you with any degree of certainty who said that. But by and large, some were against, some were for. And then the chairpersons provided additional explanations, tried to persuade people to accept the proposal and for the Prijedor public security station to be separated from Banja Luka. And as the meeting evolved, they became more and more successful in persuading the employees to agree for the public security station to become the centre. In that, the salaries were the strongest argument. That was what won the majority of people over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did somebody call your names during the debate?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In hindsight, I believe that that debate lasted for an hour. There were a lot of people. There were a lot of participants. And all the employees were there, at least those who were at the time in the building of the public security station in Prijedor. Only those on-duty officers were in their workplaces. The on-duty officer at the door and the on-duty communications officer, whoever was at the door, called me by the name and told me that my employee, the duty officer in my service, wanted to see me. He could not have called me on the phone because there was no telephone in the conference room. When my name was called, I knew that there must have been a technical problem. I left the meeting. I went upstairs. The duty officer at the time was Dusko Sarac. The duty communications officer told me that he had problems, he had received a dispatch. And judging by the urgency sign, he had to forward it very urgently, and he was supposed to forward it to Hasan Talundzic, our chief, but also to three public security stations which were in Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, and Bosanska Dubica. Some technical problems arose, and for those -- for that reason, he could not forward this dispatch as urgently as was required, and that's why he wanted my advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me interrupt you just for a moment. The question is why did your duty officer have to send this dispatch to the three municipalities that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Because a communications duty officer has to scrutinize the title of the dispatch. This has "CSB to all." That means that he is supposed to send this dispatch to all the public security stations in Bosnia and Herzegovina and their respective chiefs. And then "SJB to all" public security stations to all in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since we in the technical organisation of communications, are organised in such a way that a dispatch that arrives in Prijedor - the one, for example, in Sarajevo - is sent to the centres, centres then in turn send them to public security stations. So according to the "SJB to all," that meant that he was supposed to forward this dispatch to the three public security stations that I've just mentioned; Novi Grad or Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, and Sanski Most. And this is where the technical problem arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please continue with your explanation, where you left it off.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: When I saw what the technical problem was all about, I knew what it was, and that problem could have been handled in several ways and the transmission could be done in different ways. In addition to very urgent, there is also the word -- the letter S, the dispatch was coded. That means that this dispatch had to be encrypted before sending. And since he couldn't send it according to the same system, he had to use a different system. There are different systems with different degrees of reliability and the different time that needs to be invested in order to carry out the task. And this duty officer was afraid that he would make a mistake, and that's why we called me, as his superior officer. And in order for me to understand the degree of urgency of that dispatch, I had to skim through it. Me and all my other employees have the right to read a dispatch if need may be to do so, but we are not allowed to communicate the contents of that -- of any of such dispatches. So I looked at the dispatch in order to decide what the encoding system I should use. However, when I skimmed through the dispatch and when I saw its contents, and when I saw all the bullet points, they all came as a shock, and especially the last one, the beginning of combat activities and where the army is mentioned. And that meant something terrible for me. That was, for me, the beginning of war. Us against people from the same body of people, sometimes against brother, other people in the police, in the army, our comrades, our colleagues. We are too small to be considered a real army. The police force is a small force. This was something terrible for me. It was shocking. At the same time, I knew the rules, the rule for us to carry out our tasks. "Very urgent" means that something has to be forwarded really very urgently. There are other codes for the dispatches. The slowest dispatch is 8 hours, and the most urgent dispatch is something that is marked as "SJB to all," in other words, to Hasan Talundzic in this specific case. So this was -- this required a great degree of urgency. I had to go back to the meeting, and my communications duty officer could not leave his workplace. And I told him exactly which system to use to forward this dispatch. And because of the urgency of the dispatch, I took the so-called book of dispatches, and that is the record of all the telegrams that have been received and that have been forwarded with all the details; who it was received from, who it was forwarded to, and finally the signature of the person who received the dispatch. I didn't have the time to enter this dispatch, and I was not in the position to do that. There was the duty officer who was supposed to do that. However, I took that book and that dispatch, and together with that book, I took it down to the meeting. There are my employees sitting in the front row, and I called one of them. I told Mirsad Sahuric, he was the closest to me, I told him can you enter this dispatch in the book, and can you hand it over to the chief. These are very short operations. It can be done by a skillful worker in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, can I just interrupt you for a minute here. What is the ethnic background of the employee to whom you gave the dispatch to give it to the chief?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mirsad Sahuric, and it is clear from the name that he is a Muslim. At that moment, it was not important for me whether he was a Muslim or a Serb. He was the closest to me, and that's why I gave the dispatch to him. I could have given it to anybody else, but he was the closest to me sitting, and he was a Muslim in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what Sahuric did. It took him a minute or two minutes or three minutes: He gave the dispatch to the chief, and he signed the receipt, but the meeting I could sense was drawing to an end, and I could tell that a conclusion had been reached and people were very happy that they would receive their salaries. That was the bottom line. But I was under the influence of that dispatch, and I was one of the authorised, among other, authorised officials. There were no lay citizens. This was one of our internal meetings, and we could discuss any of our internal business matters there. So I thought it was -- I had the right to ask the floor. I had not asked the floor before, I was just listening. And what I told was the following. I can't really quote my words, but I can remember the meaning of my words, exactly what I meant. I said what people were talking about, that is the chairperson, the way they promised salaries and what they -- all the good things that they promised is in contradiction with other things, and that is the same Sarajevo for which they said would send us salaries is now giving us tasks that, to my mind, look like a war, a real war, war with the army, us amongst ourselves. When I say "us amongst ourselves," I meant people in Prijedor Municipality. I never went any further because Prijedor is what I know. That's my home turf. And what I read from that dispatch was that we were supposed to either fight amongst ourselves or with the army in Prijedor. And I found that to be atrocious, to be terrible. And that's exactly what I said. This is horrible. This is something we cannot accept. And most probably what these people are saying, what they are promising to us has no grounds because the situation is totally different. And then they started asking me, "Where did you get this idea from?" "How can you say a thing like that?" And then I said, well, this is what the chief has just received, this dispatch, shows it clearly. The police -- so the policemen were there, and there were some people from the criminal police. They started shouting, "Read us the dispatch. Read where it says that." And then the chairpersons took the dispatch. They read it, and they debated amongst themselves silently, and only -- even though they were only 3 or 4 metres away from me, I couldn't hear what they were saying. A couple minutes later, they decided that the dispatch should be read, and they gave the dispatch back to Mr. Kecan, who was taking the minutes, for him to read the dispatch. He stood up. And he started reading the dispatch. As he went on reading, the noise increased in the conference room. There were no physical incidents, but there was a commotion in the conference room. And then at the end, when the dispatch had been read, people started leaving the room. Then the president of the municipality rose to his feet, that is Mr. Cehajic, and he said, "This is just a fabrication, this can't be true, and I'm leaving this meeting," and he went. But Mirza Mujadzic acted totally differently. He said, Hold on, people, we will agree. This is not -- you haven't understood this. This is not what you think it is. It's something totally different, so his reaction was totally different. He tried to keep the people in the room and continue the debate, but he failed. People scattered. People left the room. And after some time, I arrived home. And later on, I didn't hear anything about this dispatch or anything in connection with this dispatch. I only know that on that same evening, I was asked to, by somebody, I don't know who, to come back because my police needed assistance. So whenever they needed me, they would tell my duty officer to find me, and I, as head of the department, I had to be on call for 24 hours, around the clock. Wherever I went, I had to inform my duty officer where I was because if there was a need for to find me, they could find me. So that happened on that same evening. They invited me and I went there. On the following morning -- during that night, people gathered, and on the following morning, there was a takeover without a single bullet fired as far as I could hear. Some two days later, maybe, Prijedor had already been taken over. Simo Drljaca replaced Hasan Talundzic. He was now the chief. And he asked me to come to his office, and I went there. And he told me -- there were two or three other people present there. I didn't know them. I didn't know any of them. And he told me, "These are journalists from the local newspaper Kozarski Vjesnik" and he asked me -- I don't know what they were talking about before that, but he asked me whether I had a copy of that dispatch. And I told him that no, I didn't have it, because I only make one copy and I forward it to the addressee. But since there is a tape on which the dispatch is received, that's a part of the encoding system, and that is usually put into a sack, and that sack, when that sack is full, some -- within seven or ten days, then this sack is burned by my employees. So I told him, this happened some two or three days ago. The sack must still be there. It hasn't been burned. The contents of the sack have not been burned and that tape is probably still there. So he told me, okay, see if it's there. If the tape is there, make a copy and bring it to me. I gave this task to my employees, they found the tape of the dispatch, and that dispatch I brought to Simo and handed it over to him. Let me just make a remark. This machine has the following technical characteristic: If it receives a dispatch from a participant in the communication, then the letters are vertical. When somebody sends a dispatch to a different participant, then the letters are leaning towards the right. And when I or somebody else takes the tape and makes a new copy in the room, that copy will have letters leaning to the left. The copy that I have here in front of me has letters leaning to the left, so this must be a copy -- I don't know how you came by it, but I believe that this is a copy that -- the copy that I made and handed over to Simo Drljaca. But the paper that I see on the ELMO here, I can see that these letters are vertical, so these are not two identical copies. But I don't know. This is just my technical observation. This may not even be important, but this is just my observation, something that I've observed. And that's how this dispatch, from what I could see later on...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps so the transcript is clear, the record should reflect that the document on the ELMO that the witness referred to is an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to be quite clear, on the ELMO we can see a document only in part reflecting the order, paragraphs 1 through 3, whereas the document in B/C/S, maybe it's the English page number 2, has an additional paragraph number 4. But to be honest, I did not really understand. How is it possible that you told us that in the beginning, when you send a message, the letters are leaning to the right-hand side, and then making a copy, they are leaning to the left-hand side, or is it in-built into the machine as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is the machine TX 200, produced by the Electroindustrija Nis. So that is TX 200 made by Nis. It is a copy of an original French machine. This text here, this text here, I apologise, maybe my eyesight is deceiving me, but as far as I can tell, the letters are leaning to the left. This looks like a paper from the original sender, and I don't know where you got it from. And the one in front of me here, and the letters are on the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If Defence counsel could be kind enough to assist us in a better understanding of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We have in our list different listings, because in the list it says that D6 is a paper from public security station. And on the ELMO, we have a different paper. It's a paper from Territorial Defence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I just may add, I think the Court registrar gave the Court a different document than the document that the witness has. So we would like at least a couple minutes to clarify that so that our exhibit list is consistent with what the witness was testifying to and the dispatch that he received. So if we can see what the witness is looking at, it might assist us in clarifying this issue, both on the ELMO and that which is in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I think we have to attach new numbers, D6-1, D6-2, and so on. But let us proceed step by step. We can see now a document on the ELMO. And my first question would be, do you believe this is now a document leaning to the left or to leaning to the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who are you asking, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The document we have on the ELMO, on the machine on your side. Yes, this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one. I think these letters are leaning to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would mean that it's sent or received by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This dispatch, this copy here, this was certainly not sent anywhere. I think this is the original which may have come in. The chief, Hasan, after the meeting, when he went back to his office, he probably left it where he leaves his other documents, and then at some later stage, the document came. And I'm not sure where this document went through. It's outside my purview. I think this is an original, this is not a copy. And the other one, I think, is a copy from the tape we use. Not a photocopy but a tape we use in cryptographic protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Usher, to come back to the previous document. So when we look at the top of this document, is it usual or unusual that in a document in B/C/S, you can find at the top of the page the English line "Very Urgent"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We have this as a rule. All communications officers take an exam. And I've said this, and I'll specify: Every dispatch, here in this area -- a little bit to the right would be better but in the middle is also okay. It has two marks, grade of urgency and grade of secrecy. Urgency is up to who's sending to decide and the communications officer only checks it. So marks of urgency can be OB, DD, DX, and Very Urgent. These are very common things. And when a communications officer receives a dispatch like this, he must, within eight hours, that's within four hours, forward it to whoever it's addressed to. "DX," according to content, "DX" are urgent operational matters. Criminals, matters related to criminals, questioning, that sort of thing. "Very Urgent" is the most urgent dispatch there is. Sometimes they use the expression "Very Urgent," we use the expression "Very Urgent." So this is state-related information and must be forwarded as quickly as possible, even outside working hours. The police officer must go as a courier, look for the chief, and forward this to the chief. And this is a standard thing we use, Very Urgent. Every communications officer will tell you it's very common. The other mark will say O or S. That means open or coded. Now whose communication officer drafted this and why they left it out, they must have been mistaken to leave out the other marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again to repeat, I understand from your testimony that it was usual that a document in B/C/S was headed by an English text indicating the degree of urgency, so it would be usual that you can read two English words in front of text in B/C/S. Correct? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's perfectly correct. Many communications officers who don't know the language don't know the meaning of this phrase, literally. But they know full well that these words mean this must be forwarded as urgently as possible to the chief, and if the chief is not actually physically present in the station, then there's a courier who runs it and brings it to the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, let us please continue with the analysis of this document. So please use the pointer on the ELMO. The first line, where it says "MUP, RBH," what does that mean, the very top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: We in the police have a rule, and all those who have taken their exams know this rule. I'm referring to the communication officers. How do you write a dispatch? How did you put a telegram together? It must have a heading in the upper left corner containing the sender. And this is different from the headings of official documents typed and sent by official mail and not through communications. So there's a difference there. And I'm speaking about this, now. There is this heading in the left upper corner "sender," and who the document is addressed to. This is something that the communication officer looks at, and these are his guidelines. He's not supposed to read the text, and if he does by accident, he is not supposed to use the information contained therein. So the first thing you get is "sender." And then who is he sending the document -- and you can read the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Number 10-70. This number here is sometimes larger, or longer. This is the code for the sender. So when a minister sends this, then there's only number 10. So if it was the chief of police or the chief of crime squad, 10-1, 10-2.
