If it's only the minister, then just 10. 70 is the ordinal number in one of the minister's books, records. Then something has been omitted here. I don't know why. Sometimes -- always you had a dash here, and then 92, for example, because we are talking about the year 1992. But this was probably a mistake. And then you have a date underneath, the 29th of April. You can see that here. The 29th of April, 1992. So it's clear who the sender is. The communications officers and all the other professionals dealing with this know it, who the document is coming from, who the sender is, from the whole of the MUP. So the police station has its own number, 3, Banja Luka centre. You knew exactly which number each of the stations had, so you could tell who the sender was. This small number here, that means sender was the minister. Now who this is being sent to. CSB, to all and to the chief. So the MUP is sending this to the Security Services Centre and to all. Those were all the security centres across Bosnia; Prijedor, Banja Luka, Doboj. There were ten all together. SUP Sarajevo, special dispatch to the SUP of Sarajevo, and then the SJB, public security stations, all of them, depending on where they were exactly. But when the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior of the -- Ministry of Internal Affairs sent something, they only sent the documents to the centres, and then the centres forwarded it on to their stations. So my communications officer reads this CSB, and he knows then that he is supposed to forward this to everyone. And I'm talking about three different public security stations; Dubica, Novi, and Sanski Most. So that's that. This means very urgent. He wasn't supposed to write dispatch, because this has been a coded message. So sometimes they neglect, they don't write that, so we the bosses insist that they do. And now you have this mark here in the upper right corner. But you know how it got there. Doesn't matter what the machine was that was used exactly. So then the actual content of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise. I didn't get the context in the upper right corner, where it reads "11 May, 1992." What's the meaning of this, please? Was it added later or...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This handwriting, I seem to be familiar with this handwriting. I'm almost certain that this was the chief's secretary. This is her handwriting. But again, I'm afraid I might be making a mistake, but I think it's Mira Topic, the secretary. This must be her handwriting. When the chief receives a dispatch, his secretary puts it, records it, in his books, in his files. So this is a dispatch that he received. So then he can sort of monitor which dispatches he has received and which he has replied to. So the secretary is in charge of keeping records. She takes it down, and she informs him. So this is the date, and this number here, 11/12, I think this is a number that refers to one of his -- to the chief's books. I'm not sure if the book is still around. And then it says 11th of May, 1992. So my assumption is on the basis of what used to be common practice over there in those offices, but I can't know for sure. But here is my assumption. I think Hasan Talundzic, the chief, probably took this dispatch, bought it back to his office after the meeting, left it there, and that evening where he went and what he did, I have no idea. But Mira, his secretary, was there outside working hours, too. But she wasn't there at that time, so she didn't record it. So probably it was just left in his office along with all the other documents. And then several days after, this is 10 or 11 days after the takeover, as you can see, probably Simo was already chief at this point. So he didn't think that this should be destroyed, this dispatch. He gave it to Mira, and he said get it on to the books and leave it there. As far as I can remember, this is Mira Topic's signature, the chief's secretary. She was Hasan's secretary but then also Simo's secretary later on. So I think that's that. It's handwriting, it has been ten years, you know, so I may have forgotten, but this handwriting is familiar, and I am 99 per cent certain that this is Mira's handwriting. But I may be wrong. I'm certainly very familiar with this handwriting. So I think that's what happened with this dispatch, this original. This is a copy of this and what I have in front of me. This was drafted by my communications officer -- officers, at Simo's request.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think the interpretation was wrong. Correct me if I'm wrong, please. The interpretation was that this dispatch was drafted by your communications officers. Was it drafted by your communication officers, the one you have in front of you with letters leaning to the left, or did your communication officers merely take it out of the machine from the coded tape?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Not drafted. They didn't write this. They found the tape in the bag which contained used tapes. And then they would wait for a sufficient number of tapes to be there so they could burn them. Such was the fate of all encrypted material. That was the MO. So only those who were in charge, who were authorised to deal with cryptographic protection, once the amount was sufficient, they could have the documents burned. That was the rule. But it happened by accident that there was not a large amount when this tape was tossed into that bag, this yellow tape. So the tape would be left behind if it was coded. So they found the tape, and probably there were many tapes there. They found this particular one. They searched, and they found this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the witness please be asked to repeat the last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have I been clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think he has clarified it. Can you just put this in front of you. Yes, put it over the other copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm afraid the interpreter didn't get the last part of the last sentence of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] The witness just said, "Is that clear, whether I was clear." So we have it in the transcript afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see nodding from the booth. Please Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the ELMO, now we have a document with letters leaning to the left. Is this the copy that was found later from the tape? It was recorded from the tape that was found in that bag by your communications officers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it due to that that, on the right-hand side, we can't see any marks in handwriting about this being recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this document was not used later on. It had no official use. This was given to a journalist. Now who made copies of it and who looked at it, I really don't know. And it doesn't matter. The chief wanted to use it for something, and he was entitled to use it for anything he liked. He was my senior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please now remove this copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just would suggest that, so the record is clear, that they both be marked. I think we previously marked the document with the handwriting in the upper right as D6, and that bears the ERN stamp, because it was used in another trial, 0063, it looks like 3909, although it's difficult to read. The copy with the letters leaning left perhaps should receive a different designation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This then should receive D6B-1. As such, admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, will you please now take the document from the ELMO, or if you can read from the ELMO directly. So can you please turn right, and you can read from the document itself, the one displayed on the ELMO. Can you read the document out to us and try to remember whether this is the same document that we discussed here today when we spoke about the meeting at the public security station in Prijedor on the 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Should I read this out loud?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already read out this part. "All security services centres, all public security stations, and the Sarajevo SUP must take all necessary measures and actions within their purview to secure implementation of the order by the commander of the Territorial Defence staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This is a bit confusing. "Within their own purview to secure implementation of the order by the commander of the Territorial Defence staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina number 02/145-1, dated the 29th of April, 1992. We hereby forward to you the original text. "Order. On the implementation of the order by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina number 02-11-327/92. Pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina number 02-11-327/92, dated 27th of April, 1992, on the withdrawal of JNA units from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina territory, and due to a violation of this decision by the Presidency and the looting -- and the incipient looting and plundering of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the former JNA, I hereby order: "1. Carry out complete and massive blocking of all roads throughout the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina where the units of the former JNA are beginning to evacuate technical equipment and materiel in direct coordination with the MUP." Page 2: "2. Block the general region and the military facilities in the general region." I think there's a mistake here. It should be military. Because here, this reads combat facilities. Because B and V are next to each other on the keyboard of the machine. So this may be a mistake. I think it's probably a mistake. It should read military. "Military facilities from which technical equipment and materiel is being evacuated. The blockade is to be set up with different kinds of formational and natural obstacles, and these should be secured for the units of Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the MUP. "3. Unannounced columns of units of the former JNA and those unescorted by the MUP must not be allowed to leave their barracks or to travel in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "4. Speed up planning and start combat operations --" this is what struck me the most -- "throughout the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These are to be coordinated with the Territorial Defence staff of the region, district, and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When planning combat operations, plan also comprehensive measures to protect the population and the property and goods owned by citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Signed by Minister for the Interior, Alija Delimustafic." Here you have the initials of the communications officer who typed this up in Sarajevo. I knew him, but I forgot now. I think his name was Dzanko Mirsad, Mirsad Dzanko. That's the reason I recognise this, it says DZZ. This is "dz." We have a special rule in telecommunications. The typing machine doesn't have the letter "dz", it only has the classical alphabet, international. So "dz" is written as "DZZ," so this DZZ means Mirsad Dzanko. Some people ask sometimes why there are no stamps on these dispatches. We have a rule not to put any stamps on this, because the communications officer is in charge of this, and when he does this, he guarantees for it. So this is a document, and the person in charge must guarantee for the document's authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Would the usher be so kind and show the witness another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is not a document that came out of your own service. And in this document again, we can see this mark "Very Urgent" but this time in B/C/S as opposed to the one we had before when the mark was in English, "Very Urgent." Will you please tell us, can you tell where this document originated, who it came from?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's all clear. On the basis of my experience, of my long experience with communications, I could -- I've laid eyes on documents sent by National Defence. I didn't learn their rules, but I'm able to recognise their documents. They use -- they use different expressions from us. They don't use "very urgent," but like the army, they use the same expressions in B/C/S; "urgent," "very urgent," with different degrees. So this is very urgent. This is the most urgent degree. According to their book of rules, they were supposed to use the B/C/S version, so that's why it says [B/C/S phrase] or"very urgent."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you just please read out the number and the date.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is sender, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry for National Defence, Territorial Defence Staff Sarajevo, number 02/145-1, Sarajevo. Dated 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The previous document that you have read out in its entirety, the heading reads: "All security services centres, public security stations, and the SUP in Sarajevo must take all necessary measures and actions from their purview to secure implementation of the order by the commander of the Territorial Defence staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina number 02/145-1 dated 29th of April, 1992. We hereby forward to you the original text."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May it be that we have different documents? Because on my document, the registration number reads 02-11-327/92. And not 145, as you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sender's number, the number in the upper corner, that's the number I've just read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So your intention is now to read out the entire document once again, from the beginning. I thought the witness has already explained this upper left-hand side part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] He explained the previous document which referred to this one I just pointed out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to know, this document is available in English translation in the moment as well? If not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We submitted this document for the translation, but unfortunately, it hasn't been finalised yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we therefore ask the witness also to be kind enough to read this document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Kindly --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, let me tell you that there is nothing unclear about numbers here. The number that I am now showing, that I am pointing to, and the number that I am pointing to now, and that is the number that His Honour has just mentioned now, that is the number of the document by which the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina addresses the Ministry of the Defence and the Ministry of the Interior, and then the Ministry of the Interior use the other number to address their subordinates, and the Ministry of Defence using this number address their subordinates, and the Ministry of the Defence, using this number, addresses its subordinates, so this is the number of the Ministry of Defence, the other is the Ministry of the Interior, and the number that they refer to is the number under which they receive the order. I believe this is clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please read the second document in its entirety, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I've read the heading already. "Pursuant to the decision of the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina number 02-11-327/92, dated 27 April 1992, on the withdrawal of JNA units from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, due to the fact that this decision of the Presidency has been violated, and that the looting of the property of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has started by the former JNA, I hereby order the following: "1. Carry out the complete and large-scale blocking of all the roads in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina by way of which the units of the former JNA have started pulling out technical equipment and materiel in direct coordination with the Ministry of the Interior. "2. Block the general sector of military facilities from which an attempt is being made to pull out technical equipment and materiel. Do this by various sorts of formation of natural obstacles which are to be provided to the units of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Ministry of the Interior. "3. Prevent the exit from the barracks to the unannounced columns of units of the former JNA unaccompanied by the MUP and prevent their travel through the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "4. Speed up the planning and begin combat operations in the entire territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and do this in coordination with the staff of the Territorial Defence of the region, the district, and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Within the planning of combat operations, also plan the measures to protect the population and property of the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Signed by the commander Colonel Hasan Efendic." And here, this is not our communications centre. This has been done by an officer whom I don't know. I don't know whose initials are these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until half past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. In the meantime -- may I ask you to bring in the witness. In the meantime, we received the Document D46 in B/C/S. Any objections to admit this document as D46B into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, D46B. May I ask the Defence to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I would kindly ask you, since we have quite a few questions to go through, can you please speed up a little and give us a bit shorter answers. That doesn't mean you don't have to explain things, but try to be shorter in your responses.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there a prison in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. In the public security station, even before the war, there was a detention room. That's a room which meets the legal requirements for such purposes; its shape, the things that are inside. Its size is 3 by 4 metres. It may be more, may be less. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Has a prison been subsequently built and is there a prison today in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the takeover of Prijedor, up to the attack on Hambarine, did the number of people brought into the public security station in Prijedor go up?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was one of average number before the 30th of April, 1992, and a somewhat higher number was between the 30th of April and the 30th of May, the date of the attack on Prijedor. And then it went up dramatically. In this middle period, the number did go up, but not significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after the attack on Hambarine, did it go up?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did, dramatically, because the ones who were detained were primarily the participants in the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was an investigation centre set up because of the increased number of detainees, that is Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that they were set up. I didn't participate in that. I don't know who set them up and how, but yes, at that time, they were set up. Personally, I didn't believe that that was the reason for setting them up, but I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Up to the takeover of Prijedor, you had meetings, so-called collegians [as interpreted], at which department heads met. When Simo Drljaca was appointed the chief of the public security station, did something change?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Very much so. Ever since I joined the police in 1980, up to the date that you have mentioned, and that is when Simo Drljaca came, there were weekly meetings chaired by the chief of the station, formerly the secretary of the station. And the members of that meeting or the collegian were all the heads of departments, and one of them -- I was one of them, one of the heads. I was the head of the communications department. When Simo came, that body ceased to exist and meet. At least, they didn't meet at regular intervals. He would, for example, call me if there was something to do, a job to do, or if he needed me to report to him on something. And sometimes he also called all the heads if there was an action envisaged for which we were all to take part in. So these were not so regular meetings of a regular body consisting of all the department heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many times a day would you enter Simo Drljaca's office on average?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Since Simo Drljaca was my direct superior, my immediate superior from whom I took orders, he gave me tasks, and I reported to him for the discharge of my duties, whenever I had to see him, I would enter his office. I would stay there for as long as needed in order to discuss the issue that I wanted to discuss. Sometimes it didn't happen at all during one day, and sometimes it would happen as many times in three days, whether it was on his invitation or I had to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever sent to do something in the investigation centres Omarska and Keraterm? And can you tell us briefly about the things that you were asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Before those times, and at the beginning of these events, I only did those things that were under my authority, and that is the maintenance of communication facilities and their regular use in the transmission of information. That is why throughout all that period, that is, in 1992, I was in Omarska three times, and once I was in the investigation centre Keraterm. I was never in Trnopolje during that period of time. I did go on a private business. I took a woman to see her sister, and that's when I went through that in my private vehicle, and I had that that woman in the vehicle. I saw the area from that vehicle, but I didn't pay too much attention to what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who provided security of these investigation centres? Could you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me first say something about Omarska. It is my opinion that the physical security was provided by active policemen who belonged to the police station in Omarska. And there were also many more other people whom I didn't know. I knew the former ones, but I didn't know the latter ones. The latter ones wore the reserve -- the uniforms of the reserve police. That's why I knew that they were reserve policemen. Sometimes reserve policemen didn't even have those blue uniforms, but they wore camouflage uniforms. And for that reason, I didn't know whether they were really military or maybe they were the police who wore camouflage uniforms because they didn't have any other uniforms. So that's for the Omarska investigation centre. I was in Keraterm only once, and the investigation centre Keraterm, the building itself is in such shape that both the detainees and the guards are separated from each other. Because the inspector who interrogated them and who had in their possession the communications means, they were in those rooms that used to house offices for that company. So there I couldn't see much. I saw police members, some of whom I knew personally. In any case, they wore uniforms, some of them. But not all of them. They were our employees. They were taking statements in these offices, but since I walked through the corridor, I didn't enter any of the offices but the one where the telephone was, I repaired it, and then I left that room. I heard that on that day, an international commission or group of international representatives were supposed to arrive on that day, and that is why everybody was well, sort of, dressed, and they were sort of better groomed. They were expecting that delegation, and they had cleaned a little. I actually can't compare how the whole thing looked like before because I was only there that one time, but there was something in the air showing that they were expecting guests. And during that period of time, I was never in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who carried out investigations in these investigation centres? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you - again I'm only talking about Omarska - I saw in Omarska our inspectors. And when I say "our," I mean the employees of the public security station in Prijedor. My task did not take me to all the offices where they worked, but those whom I saw were employees, inspectors, of the public security station. There were some employees belonging to the state security, and that is the detachment of the Banja Luka centre. And there were some unknown people, people for whom I didn't know who they were. Maybe they were the military security or some reserve forces, I don't know, or the state security. But in any case, there were people whom I didn't know. In Omarska, that is. In Keraterm now likewise, but fewer of them altogether, a fewer number of them. In Trnopolje, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, the inspectors, who did they report to? Do you know, the inspectors who carried out investigations in these investigation centres, who did they report to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I will tell you about Omarska. I don't know that much about Trnopolje. I was there for only half an hour. I went through a corridor, entered a room, and left. And as for Omarska, I stayed there for an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you went through a corridor in Trnopolje. Are you referring to Trnopolje or Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is my mistake. I was never in Trnopolje. I meant Keraterm. I'm sorry. I apologise. So in Keraterm, that used to be a ceramics factory, so the machinery used to be on the ground floor, and the inspectors were interrogating on the first floor, in the offices, and that's where I entered one of the offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to my question. To your mind and to your knowledge, since you are an employee of the public security station in Prijedor, who did the inspectors report to? That is, the public security station inspectors. And what about the state security inspectors? And if you know, who did the military security inspectors report to? If you don't know, just say so, say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe -- I actually assume that that was the case, because that used to be the situation before these events. An inspector gets a task from his superior and reports to the superior about the results of his work. The boss to all of these inspectors - so that is, of the criminal police - was Ranko Mijic, and I suppose, I expect that they reported to him. And that he was the one who then reported to the chief of the police station, and that is Simo Drljaca. I never witnessed the reporting chain. I didn't need to. But on several occasions, I had an opportunity -- I could see Ranko Mijic entering Simo's office. Sometimes I couldn't enter Simo's office because Ranko was already there, so I had to go back and return later on if I needed to talk to him. As for the state security, they had their own boss, their own superior. And according to the rules, they reported to their own boss who also had a boss in Banja Luka. And as for the others, I believe that they also had their own boss. I don't know who that was. I don't know who they were, where they came from. I never observed their work. They were completely unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about conversations with people in Kozarac prior to the outbreak of the conflict, and who led those conversations through your communications?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's difficult to specify the date. I don't remember, but I think it may have been the third decade [as interpreted] of the month of May. Our police department participated in the activities of the people of Kozarac. The department was led by the former head of the department Osme Didovic. The phone connections were in a bad state. Many of the phone lines were down, so they used the police shortwave frequency, and the communications centre where I work, the conversations were being monitored all the time, so I was in a position to, just in passing -- you know, I wasn't sitting there all the time, listening in, but in passing I did overhear a number of conversations. During the period I'm referring to, that's between the 20th and the 30th of May, there were attempts by the army. I know several times I heard him on the line. I couldn't quite recognise his name, but he said his name, Captain Zeljaja. And he tried to have -- to reach an agreement with the other side, a nonviolent agreement with no fighting and no one getting hurt, to reach a peaceful agreement and avoid conflict. Osmet Didovic, the commander of the department, would always talk back to him. And whenever Zeljaja wanted something or asked for something, Didovic would always tell him: "You know, I'm talking to you from a vehicle and I'll pass the message on to our superiors." And I think the highest ranking superiors was the head of the military sector -- section, Medunjanin. I think that was his name. And he always told Zeljaja that he would see about this with Medunjanin, and then he would get back to him. In our communications centre at my command table, I had a special device which identified the number calling, and I could tell that he wasn't calling from a moving vehicle, but rather from a station. I suppose he was lying because he was trying to buy some more time. After a while, he would call and say that's what was said and this was not what was said and whether they agreed or not, I didn't really feel the need to -- I didn't really belong to the military communications. I was in the police communications. I didn't feel I should be part of that. I'm just saying that's what this commander was saying, and that wasn't right. And then afterwards, what ensued was the fighting in that particular area. I was not there during this period. I don't know any details, but you could see later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to meet Dr. Stakic? And if so, can you tell us when, on what occasion, and what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet him, but I didn't get to know him very well. I remember the first time I saw him. I didn't really have to cross the street to the other building, the Municipal Assembly building officially very often. And I was not a member of any party, as I've already said. I remember distinctly it was outside the Municipal Assembly building. He wanted me to fix Mico Kovacevic's TV since I was an electronic engineer. So I met Mico Kovacevic outside the Municipal Assembly. He was walking with Dr. Stakic, and that's the first time I saw him. Mico and I started talking, and he asked me when I would fix the TV. Dr. Stakic didn't say a single word. He was just standing there. I don't remember if we were formally introduced, but I noticed Dr. Stakic then on that occasion. He wouldn't have stuck in my mind really for anything. I wouldn't be able to tell him from Adam were it not for the fact that he was quite young and bald at the same time. He was quite silent, and he looked at me and he looked at Mico and he didn't say anything. As far as his last name, I don't have a good mind for last names, those that don't matter to me. The only reason I remember is that my mother's maiden name is Stakic, although it's not the same family. I'm from East Bosnia, from around Brcko, that's 2 kilometres to the east, and he's from that area, but that was my mother's maiden name so that's why I memorised it. So the only thing I remember was that his last name was Stakic and that that was the man. I remember he was wearing a yellow jacket with some white fur. That's all I remember. I may have seen him two or three times later on, but he was not important to me. So we'd just say hello sometimes, but apart from that, we never formally met afterwards. He didn't ask me anything, and I didn't ask him anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember if you had ever met Dr. Stakic prior to the takeover, the time you met him with Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was prior to the takeover.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dr. Stakic in Simo Drljaca's office, Simo Drljaca whom you met every day in his office?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I didn't see him in Simo's office. I never stayed in Simo's office for a long time. But I would enter the police building, and I would go out always on my own private -- on my own business officially. I never met him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never met him in the public security station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't remember ever having met him there inside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about the existence of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know at this time who its members were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. We, employees of the police, we stick to our job. We know the hierarchy, we know the chain of command, we know who we are supposed to report to and what we are supposed to do. It is not even desirable to maybe look around myself too much. I never felt the need. I wasn't interested in finding out who the Crisis Staff were, who was on the Crisis Staff, and what they were doing. Experience teaches, even in the socialist system, that even for minor things they'd immediately set up staffs, Crisis Staffs and other kinds of staffs. I had the feeling that officials were doing this kind of thing just to make minor things seem more important than they actually were. I never attached much importance to these various staffs. I was never really interested nor did I know who were members of the staff. You know, it's like you have a Crisis Staff somewhere far away in a different town. That's what it was like for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've asked you already and you've told me that you never received orders from the Municipal Assembly or the Executive Board. Now, let me just ask you, did you ever receive any orders from the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly between April and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1993, at the beginning of 1993, Simo Drljaca left the Prijedor public security station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: He went to Bijeljina for a while, and then after that, he was back. I know that he did leave but I wouldn't know about the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Bogdan Delic did. When he left, Bogdan Delic became chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, was Simo Drljaca demoted or promoted, in case you know where he had gone to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he did exactly. He went to Bijeljina, and the MUP was in Bijeljina at this point. What he was doing over there, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say the MUP, you mean the ministry, the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. They had their headquarters for Republika Srpska in Bijeljina. I even can't remember -- you know, ministers kept changing. I can't even remember who was occupying the position during that particular period, and I can't remember who it was. Whether he was in that group or what he was doing, I don't know and no one ever told me. It wasn't really important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you work in the public security station in Prijedor in 1993, and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the reasons that I wasn't really interested so much in what was going on is that my illness kept deteriorating in those months. That's the second half of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was a mistake. That was towards the end of 1993 and the beginning of 1994, my illness deteriorated. And then in March 1994, I left for Belgrade to neurology, and I was undergoing examinations, medical examinations for about 40 days, and then in June an operation was performed on one of my eyes that was giving me trouble. And then I was on sick leave, and I didn't come back until the end of the war. It was only at the end of 1997 that I came back to my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... [In English] another exhibit. It's not marked yet. It's a detailed plan of Prijedor city with the MUP building and Municipal Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I come back to the last document you tendered. This was the one 145, signed by Mr. Hasan Efendic. My understanding is that you tendered this document. This would then be D48B. Any objections by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then admitted into evidence. And in the list of evidence, please make reference to the transcript that we know that we have the translation in the transcript. This document following now would be D49. I can see no objections, therefore, admitted into evidence. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On this sketch of the town of Prijedor, it's blown up, you have two buildings marked in green. Can you please explain which two buildings are these, and can you point to exactly where the entrance is to these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is part of an official town plan by the land surveyor's office, and it's very accurate. I think aberrations are extremely small. This building I'm pointing at right now, that's the municipality building. You can see the stairs here, the entrance and the exit to the municipal building. This is the front of the municipality, and this here is a park. And now there's a street running between the municipality building and the public security station, and this is the public security station. That's one section of the public security station because there's another section which you can't see here. Now we can see it. So one part of the station is here. These -- the garage. And the entrance to the station is right here. And this green patch, green area outside the station, this is the pavement. This is the street. This is the other side of the street and the pavement, and this is the municipality building. And this here is a green area, and this is a street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just before we leave this document, may I ask you, have there ever been cells or arrest cells or provisional cells behind or close to the building of the security building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The building itself, this one here that I pointed out, you can't see it here, unfortunately. This is where the map ends. But the public security building, it's here. And then behind is the garage. And here there's another garage. So it's parallel to the SUP building. Now, this is an official courtyard where vehicles belonging to the police are parked. And the only detention room in this building here behind the garage, and then on the first floor, but not on the first floor, they couldn't, but there was a room where they had meetings. So here maybe they could detain someone just for an hour or two. But I can't say this for sure. So the only detention room was the one that was the official detention room, according to the rules that had to be satisfied. That was the only thing. But here, around here, officially, there was no space for detention. Officially, certainly, there was nothing in the surroundings here. The municipality building, the park, this is the museum. This is the museum. Here is the court next to the SUP building. This is the building where the mine management was located. This, again, is a green area. And then this last building, which also belongs to the public security station, that's the last building I'm talking about, and that's where the room was that I've referred to, the detention room. Three by four metres perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you why you emphasise that officially there was nothing in the surroundings for the purposes of detention? Was there something unofficially or is it really your testimony that all the time all over 1992, there was only one room for detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I said "officially." I want to tell you the truth, so I'm trying to limit myself to the area that really is related to. That's throughout the ten years of my work there, that's what I can talk about. There was that one room which had that purpose, and that was that. Maybe they may have used one of the other rooms or the hall for that at some point, but all the other rooms were occupied, the warehouses, the garage. So there was no space inside any of those rooms to detain anyone. Those were very small rooms. Maybe only the hall, but then again the hall, but you can't keep it shut for a long time because there were glass windows which would be easy to shatter if someone was trying to get. So there were no such facilities available really. I'm trying to be very cautious here because someone may have detained someone without me knowing about it, obviously. But those were private things. I'm telling you what there was in official terms. Not that I know of anything unofficial that was happening, but this is the only thing I know for sure. That's why I'm saying "official."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you have further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] No, Your Honour. We have finished our direct examination. [Interpretation] Mr. Jankovic, you will now answer questions by my learned colleague from the Prosecution and after that also by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As to the fact that during a period of time of two hours hearing, there is mandatory break for the change of the videotapes, I think it's appropriate, in order not to interrupt the cross-examination and the following questions and the re-examination, that we have a short break of about five minutes just in order to give the possibility to the video unit to exchange the tape now, if there is no other order by the video unit. It's okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would say I think I have a couple of hours of cross-examination. About two hours would be my estimate, if that's permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, but nevertheless we have to make a break, and it's better to start with a break. --- Break taken at 2.17 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And may the Prosecution start with the cross-examination, but may I ask to be as brief as possible, that we have, to a certain extent, a balance between the parties also during the Defence case. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. You said that "we stick to our job," discussing the police, and that "we had our own chain of command." Perhaps you could explain something to me. On the 29th of April, I gathered from your testimony, you recognised your boss as Mr. Hasan Talundzic. On the 30th of April of 1992, the next day, I gather that you recognised as your boss Simo Drljaca and you no longer followed the orders of Mr. Talundzic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, since Mr. Talundzic was the police chief that had been elected by the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, that was elected in the 1990 elections consisting of all nationalities, who was it that told you -- or under whose orders, whose orders were you following --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It is wrongly stated that Mr. Talundzic was elected by the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it can be appropriate to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Talundzic was nominated by the party that had won the most seats - thank you; Mr. Lukic is absolutely correct - and that was the SDA party. And under the agreement among the parties, his name was forwarded to the Ministry of the Interior and he was named the chief of police of Prijedor. Is that correct, sir? I see you nodding, but you have to answer out loud so that the record includes your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I understand your question. Yes, in our service, all the heads, higher heads, are appointed by the minister, and that was also the case with Mr. Talundzic. And whose proposal that was upon, that really doesn't matter. Obviously, it was on the proposal of a party. I report to my superior, and I obey my superior. My superior was Talundzic. On the day when the dispatch arrived, I gave it to Talundzic, who signed it and took it from me. On the following day, at 7.00 in the morning, the -- Prijedor was taken over. I was not into politics. I did not participate in the takeover. How that happened, I don't know. But physically, Talundzic was no longer there. There was another man whom I had seen for the first time the day before and on that day for the second time. And he told me, "I am the chief." And what else was I supposed to do? I saw everybody else reporting to him and taking his orders. What was I supposed to do? Everybody else did it, I did it as well. What do you think, that I could do differently than everybody else? I am a person with a degree in electrical engineering. I worked for the police. What am I supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And you're not an trial here. I'm not accusing you of anything, and I appreciate you just --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I am trying to defend my case, if you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, so this man who introduced himself as the new chief of police was Simo Drljaca. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And you knew that Simo Drljaca was not a professional policeman; he had been an administrator in the schools prior to that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I told you then, on the eve of the takeover was when I saw him for the first time. I didn't know who he was, what he was. He only told me "I am Simo Drljaca." That's what I knew. Then later on, I heard that he worked in education, that he was a lawyer for the education system or something. But I didn't need to know anything more about that. It was not up to me to know anything more of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. But obviously, this must have a very memorable event; you come to work one day and the chief has been replaced, all the top officials in the municipality have been replaced. Didn't you talk about this with your fellow employees as to who it was that had ordered this takeover?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The first part is correct, what you have said. Obviously, it is a memorable day when my chief changes, and that I remember. However, the municipality building being so close is still very far. I never asked any questions as to who ordered it, what was ordered. I just assumed there were people there. What people those were, I don't know. I really don't know who these people were, but I believe that there must have been an organisation because this person appeared in front of all of us, all the employees of the police. I was just one of the two hundred and something employees of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I don't want to waste your time or my limited time asking you about things you don't know. Would it be correct, then, you don't know who Mr. Drljaca was receiving his orders from? You never attended any meetings of the Crisis Staff or meetings in which the military was present. Is that correct? And you do not know who set up the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: You've asked me a lot of things at a time. First, answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, if I forget a question, can you please repeat it. So the first question was this: Did I know who appointed Simo? Answer, no. He appeared on that evening for the first time, and he said, "I am your chief." He said that in a very authoritative voice. And who was any of us to ask him, "Okay, who appointed you? How come you're now our chief?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and slow down a little bit in order to allow the interpreters to follow your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm doing my best, but sometimes I forget myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps to assist, I'll break down my question. You're correct, I asked you several questions together. Did you ever attend any meetings of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever -- do you know who was giving orders? Did you read or were you present in meetings in which orders were given to Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, like before that time, orders did not come via written telegrams, mostly not. But I never came across any of them. There may have been such telegrams, but I never came across any. If there were any, I usually don't read those telegrams without a need for me to read them. I never saw any orders issued to Simo, but I believe that there were orders, and I believe that they came from his superior and his superior is in the centre, in Banja Luka. His superior is the chief of the security centre in Banja Luka. We were just a branch office, so to say. So it was my assumption, and I didn't go anywhere else, anywhere further to corroborate my assumptions. I did not need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. But right now I'm not asking you about what you assumed but what you actually saw or witnessed or read. Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I didn't read them. I never experienced anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever read any reports written by Simo Drljaca to the Crisis Staff or to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any meetings in which Mr. Drljaca coordinated with military counterparts?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I believe you told us you've never been in the Municipal Assembly -- let me rephrase that. You never were in Dr. Stakic's office and never attended any meetings with Dr. Stakic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to make a mistake here. I don't know where his office was. I don't know where his position was. But I was once in a room, but that was long before, immediately after the first multiparty elections, and I was called by Dr. Mico Kovacevic. There were other people there whom I didn't know. I don't know. I believe that this was his party. I don't know whose room it was. Now, if you ask me whether that was a meeting of some sort, an organised meeting, I don't know. I just can tell you that I was invited, I went there, and left. And the SDS was supposed to propose three candidates for the commander of the public security station because the SDA proposed the chief, Talundzic. And since these people didn't understand much about the police, they didn't know the people, they only asked me about my opinion. If I was in the position to propose somebody, who would I propose? And then I proposed -- there were some candidates, a lawyer from the health centre who was an alcoholic, or at least looked like an alcoholic to me; the second one was Simo Drljaca, I remembered his name, I didn't know him; and there is also Dusan Jankovic, the assistant commander in our station. I proposed Dusan Jankovic for one and only reason; he was the only professional among the three and it was in the interest of the service. And I thought as a professional, he would do the best job, unlike the other two whom I didn't know and who were not professionals. That was my only reason for proposing him. Whether Dr. Stakic was there at the time or not, I don't know. If he was there, I assure you I didn't see him. Maybe he was there, but in any case, I didn't see him. And that is throughout the entire period, that is the only time when I entered the premises of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, who took power on the 30th of April? Who was in charge of Prijedor that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can just give you my impressions. I wouldn't go in depth because I may make a mistake. On the 29th, I told you what happened with that dispatch. After that, I went home. In the evening, my subordinates called me, and I've already explained what the system was when they needed to call me. The duty officer had to be aware of my whereabouts 24 hours a day. And those who wanted to get in touch with me, my superior or somebody else, they would get in touch with the duty operations officer who would then call me. And that's what happened on that day. Somebody called me. I don't remember who that was, because the duty operations officer changed all the time. There was somebody else on duty at different times. So I went to the communications centre, and I was told that an order had arrived to go to Cirkin Polje at the entrance to Prijedor, and to go there to the local commune premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I left two communications officers behind, and the rest of us went there, all of us, because somebody had to be left behind. Somebody has to be in the communications centre all the time. On that night, we all stayed there, and then on the following morning, when Prijedor had been taken over, we returned, and we came to the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, it's a very simple question: Do you know who took power on the 30th of April? Can you give us the names of the individuals or the organisation who took power?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you who the organiser was, because there were a lot of people gathered there. All those people who were gathered there were employees of the public security station, and there were some other people unknown to me. But there were also reserve policemen whom I also didn't know. I didn't know them. So there were lots of unfamiliar people. It was night. I didn't have anything whatsoever to do directly with any of them. There were a lot of people. And as for the organisation, nobody said anything about that. And I was not interested in that. I just was one among that huge mass of people. I saw all of my bosses there, and I just joined them. I just went with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, in fact, you didn't see all of your bosses there. You didn't see Mr. Talundzic, for example, there. You only saw Serbian police officers there in Cirkin Polje. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And in Cirkin Polje, there was a house where the leaders were at. Is that true? Were you invited into a house where the leaders were staying?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you be more precise? The leaders of what? Are you referring to the public security station or maybe wider?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In Cirkin Polje, did you see Slobodan Kuruzovic that night, the early morning hours of the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I would recognise Slobodan Kuruzovic even today. He may have been there. Why? Because there were people wearing military uniforms, people with ranks. But I didn't know them. A major approached me and asked for the radio set. I refused to give it to him because he didn't belong to the police station. I told him, You're not on my list, on the list of the police station. And I don't know which major that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see Dr. Stakic in Cirkin Polje that night?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you asked to remain outside or did you go into a residence there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I entered the building, but as a communications officer, I did not have any concrete tasks in these activities. Then one of the superiors -- when I say "superiors," I always refer to the superiors or the heads of the public security stations. That is one of my colleagues, in other words. He gave me a small package, sir. You don't see me, sir. I'm showing the size of the package. So he gave me this kind of package and told me these are the forms for the new official IDs, that is the IDs that every policeman needs to carry on their body. So he told me these are new forms, and if there's nothing else for you to do, please fill out these forms. So I took a pencil, and they came to me, the old policemen, the new policemen. There was a lack of professionalism there because there was no photo. I just asked them what their names were; when they told me their names, I would enter their name on the ID, and God knows how many names I entered on that night. When they approached me, told me their names, I would just enter them on the forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Believe me, sir, I do find everything you say interesting, but because we're limited in time, try to answer the question accurately in as short a manner as you can do and still be accurate. So you entered the building briefly. Would that be correct? My question originally was Did you go inside the building? and I believe your answer was yes, you did, but just briefly to fill out these forms, to get these forms.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But there were lots of rooms there, and I was sitting in one of them, and believe me it could happen if did happen. I didn't know what was going on in the other rooms, and I was filling out these forms for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, that explains things. And I won't ask you further questions on this subject in the interest of time. I want to go back to talk about the visits of Stojan Zupljanin first in April. At that time, were you aware that an Autonomous Region of Krajina had been set up, based in Banja Luka, prior to the time that Stojan Zupljanin came to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: All these political terms, Autonomous Region, independent, not independent, I really never found that interesting. I never watched any TV programmes. I didn't read newspapers. And it was something that looked to me like it really didn't happen. And I have the same attitude to the current political events. I knew Stojan Zupljanin from the university days. For me, he was the chief of the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, and that's how I know him and that's why he matters to me. Everything else doesn't matter a thing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When Mr. Zupljanin came to Prijedor, he wanted the officers in Prijedor to change the emblems that they wore and to sign a loyalty oath to the Serbian Republic. Is that correct? Or please correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe in some other sense it means that, because the centre in Banja Luka covered - I don't want to be wrong on the number of municipalities - but it did cover a certain number of municipalities. And this entire area covered by the Banja Luka centre, in all of these municipalities, there were -- there was the SDS was the party in power, which appointed a chief, and only in four municipalities it was the SDA. And the objective was for the centre to remain unique because these four municipalities did not all belong to Prijedor. They were scattered all over the area. And if they remained there, and if the centre accepted those insignia, then obviously it was assumed that we would also wear these insignia. But that's what I believe was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can you just very briefly describe the insignia that they wanted you to wear.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A three-coloured flag; red, blue, and white. And not a square but a wavy sort of line, as if that flag was sort of in the wind, and the size of it was of a stamp, 2 times 3 centimetres, as far as I can remember. I saw it then. Very few people wore those insignia for a very short period of time, so...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the 29th of May, the meeting that you talked about, all the employees were there. And is it correct that the debate at that time was whether Prijedor would answer only to Banja Luka, which was controlled at that time by the SDS party, or would answer to Sarajevo and to the interior minister, who at that time was a member of the SDA party, or how Prijedor police would resolve this dilemma that they were getting orders from two parties who were in opposition to each other?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Very complicated question. Firstly, I believe that you made a mistake; you said 29th of May but I believe you meant the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, let's move on then. I think that the debate was still on, and the situation was still the following: What is being said and what is being meant between the lines was, Why should we be with Banja Luka if Banja Luka doesn't send us salaries? Why should we be used by Banja Luka? We would be better off by being with Sarajevo. This is what the chairpersons were saying, and they said we would receive the first salary on the following day, and the second one, the back payment would follow within a few days. That's what they were saying. But the motive among these top people was not to be concerned about our salaries, but there were other people who understood it that way. So let me put it this way: One thing was said, and what was meant was something else. That was the situation at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the middle of that meeting to resolve this problem, you say you received the telegram that we looked at earlier today. And this was a telegram that was addressed to all the security services centres, to all the public security stations throughout Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that when you read this, although it's normally not your practice to read telegrams, you had to comment on it at the meeting because of its importance and what you felt what it meant, that it would mean war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As a communications officer, I am not forbidden to read such documents. We can do them in -- that in justified cases. But if I do read the contents of such a telegram, I am not to abuse my knowledge. So I had the right to read the telegram, and I thought I had to read it because of the urgency. So that's the first part of your question. And now, can you please repeat the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you read the telegram, you felt that it was of great importance; you needed to tell others about it because it would mean war, such an order. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because of the very short period of time that could be measured in minutes only. I really didn't have the time to think about the consequences of me saying something or of me not saying anything. I wanted to keep the level head, but I really didn't have the time. I still don't think that I made a mistake by speaking out. But as for the consequences, what they were -- but it was my feeling that I had to ask the floor and contribute to the discussion, to the debate, because it was an internal meeting, the people there were only members of the police. So I didn't speak before the public at large. I didn't release anything to the public. I spoke in front of my fellow policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And is it correct, as you mentioned, there are two different ways in which telegrams are classified, if I understood you correctly. One is the urgency of the telegram, and second is secrecy, and this telegram was not marked secret. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct; no, it wasn't marked as secret. And ever since I have been in this position, I have experienced this mark being omitted. And all the time bosses punish their subordinates if they omit this mark of secrecy. Each today, you can go to the service, you can still see telegrams without the mark of secrecy although there should be one. You can see that even today in Banja Luka security centre. That is something that people tend to omit. That is a misdemeanour or breach of discipline that happens very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Try to just answer the question, just so that we can finish on time today. It was not marked secret. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned that just in the Banja Luka region, there were municipalities that were controlled by -- not by the SDA but by the SDS, that the majority of municipalities were not controlled by Muslims, and the chief of police in these places were Serbs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I could enumerate all the municipalities. I do know this because I still work with those municipalities. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to shorten the list a little bit, because I believe you would have about 17, the three municipalities that you mentioned you would have to forward it to, Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, and Bosanska Dubica, all three of those on the 29th of April, 1992, had Serbian chiefs of police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. No, no, excuse me. Novi Grad, Bosanski Novi, and Bosanska Dubica I think had Serb chiefs. And Sanski Most, I'm not sure really about Sanski Most. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now given what was written in this telegram, in point number 4 that you read, it basically says to accelerate the planning and launching of combat activities. Did you find it surprising that this would be sent to chiefs of police openly including many, the majority, who were members of Serbian nationality and many of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe this was -- I have given it some thought. I believe this was poor quality work in terms of delivery of information. Starting from Sarajevo, because that was the source of information, and I'm referring here to the Ministry of the Interior, when you organise the delivery of information, it's about the technical makeup of the whole channel. From Sarajevo, from the MUP, information is being sent out to ten different centres, these dispatches. And then each of these centres in their turn forwards this information to public security station, to public security stations. Only Prijedor had three, and Banja Luka I think must have had 10 or 11 at the time. And then due to the poor quality of their work, they know that they have the SDA in Prijedor. And they send it over there. So now why didn't they pay attention, these other three municipalities, I really don't know. A communications officer has a limited job, after all. He looks at the heading, CSB to all, SJB to all, he just looks at it, and he does what it says. And then there is a discrepancy between that and the real situation on the ground in Prijedor, between how something is technically implemented and how information is delivered and what actually happens. So there you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a very specific question: The first line, the first addressee is to "Chief, all security services centres." For the Banja Luka region, that would have been Stojan Zupljanin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when you were going over the addressing of this telegram and the numbering system, at one point you said something is omitted, something that is supposed to be there. What was that? What is omitted from the addressing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The dispatch number was omitted. You have MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then you have 10-70, and then nothing following. 10 means minister. 70 is the number of entry in the minister's book of records, the ordinal number of the dispatch that was sent. And then there's a slash, and the slash is supposed to be followed by the year the dispatch refers to. So the number 92 is missing, if you ask me. And as a rule, it should be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, this order also instructs the recipients to stop the JNA from pulling out its materiel and equipment from Bosnia. I know you've said you don't follow political events, but the 29th of April, correct me if I'm wrong, was after the recognition of Bosnia by the European Union and the United States. And at this time, isn't it true that it was the SDS party that did not want the JNA to remove its equipment from Bosnia and it was the Muslim and Croat parties that did want the JNA to leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a really complicated political issue. Too complicated for me, I think. Last time I testified - that was a year and a half ago - believe me, a colleague of yours asked me when exactly Bosnia and Herzegovina became an independent sovereign state. Frankly, I didn't know the date. Later, I asked around and they told me that it was, I think, the 6th of April or thereabouts. So being a technical person, an engineer, I really know precious little about all these things. I feel a certain amount of commotion surrounding certain events, but there are too many technical things, and my hard disk in my head has an overload of information, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I can understand that. Sir, based upon what you did with the telegram you received, would there be any way for what you received to have been in the hands of Vladimir Arsic on the night of the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe the telegram could not have been, but that someone who was there may have overheard something and then passed the information on to him. That seems possible. Why? Hasan was the chief. I suppose he took it, but I don't think he passed it on to anyone who might have given it to Arsic. I don't know what he did with it, but on that particular day I suppose he was there. But I really don't know because he took the document -- he took it over in front of 500 people, I suppose, or thereabouts, 500 people present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Later, someone - Mr. Drljaca - asked you for a copy of this, and later you saw it, am I correct, it was published in Kozarski Vjesnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear the demands for the surrender of weapons from the Muslim communities, places like Brdo, like Hambarine, and places like Kozarac and the surrounding villages? Did you ever hear public demands for them to surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe I did. When I say "I believe I did," I mean lately I've heard stories about those things happening back then. When I think back, I seem to remember that there was something like that, but there were so many events happening almost simultaneously, you know, weapons and my own job with communications and this and that. I can't remember and I can't be sure, but yes, I think there was something like that. Recently I heard someone talk about it, so that sort of rang a bell, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear announcements made in Prijedor on any subject in the name of the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. At this time, I spent most of my time, including my spare time, doing my job. And when I wasn't doing my job, I was trying to get food for my family and for myself and look after number one, but I wasn't actively involved in the town's life or public activities. And I do not know that there was ever any such announcement. I don't want to say that there wasn't one, but I certainly don't know of it. That's after the one I told you about, the one I heard on the radio where a plea was made to prevent war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned -- when you say the radio, you're now talking about a communication radio and not public radio that would play music, that type of radio station. You're talking about --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, diffusion radio, that's what I talked about, on the 10th of April when the two journalists came and when there was the announcement that everything was under control and there would be no war. That's the announcement I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And you also talked about communications with Osme Didovic, who was head of the security station in Kozarac. You said about 10 or 15 police were stationed there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Osme Didovic was not chief. We called him commander of the department, and chief would have been higher up the pecking order.
