This department, in peacetime, had between 10 and 12 active-duty policemen. As things were getting worse, they started mobilising reserve police forces, so the reserve police forces joined in. The police work in shifts, you know, so when I go there, I can't see all of them at a single time. And I didn't ask him about how many people he had. But probably at this time, as the situation was getting ever more complicated, the number of mobilised reservists kept growing, too. It was on the rise, but how many exactly at this point I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm particularly interested, and I want you to concentrate now on the 24th of May, 1992, the day of the attack on Kozarac. Did you monitor, did you hear any of the radio communications between Mr. Didovic and authorities in Prijedor such as Major Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that. This was not a diffusion radio. It was our own police radio, the same kind of radio that the police use when patrolling the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In fact, did you hear Mr. Didovic -- not the 24th, but I believe it would have been the next day, the 25th or the 26th, offer to surrender?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you to please -- because I told you in my testimony, I don't remember the date. Don't ask me the 25th, did you do something on the 25th, and then I can tell you that yes I did, and then I'm not sure. So I don't want to be tied down to any dates. I think that was during the last ten days of May. Whether it was the 25th or the 26th, I really don't know. I can't say that I remember a single sentence of that, but I remember the overall picture. I remember the more global context. I remember that Zeljaja was endeavouring to keep conflict from breaking out, to deal with this in a peaceful, nonviolent way, and then they talked back to him and they gave him their conditions, their terms. And you know, it was part of my work. I would be in the room, and then the next meeting I would be out of the room, so I wasn't there -- sitting there, really listening very attentively. My communications officer at one point told me, they still haven't reached an agreement, so that was all I knew at that time and that's what I took it to mean, they are still working on it. I can't say that I heard anything personally over the radio, but I cannot completely rule this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to your colleague Mr. Didovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that he had been killed. Now, the person I heard this from could not have been taken as a reliable source, I think. I remember his face, but where did he come from? He was wearing a huge hat, civilian clothes. But he had stars and some -- some stars on a shoulder strap. But you know, as we usually say, he's not from our village. So this person told me once, but he didn't belong to any of the units and he was just wearing civilian clothes and a huge black hat. He had the stars and the epaulets. I think he was probably crazy. He said he'd seen something. So I wouldn't take that for an official piece of information from a person like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could you share with us what this person told you happened to Mr. Didovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember as if through a dream. They were headed somewhere, and then there was a bridge, and then the police came. Some sections of the police, some active-duty policemen from Kozarac were on their way somewhere. I can't remember the details, but there was a clash and they were killed, and they remained there lying on the ground next to the river and that bridge. That's all I can tell you. But you know, I'm pervaded by this feeling of unease if I see a corpse. I'm horrified. So I don't really remember the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to break because I learned that, once again, the tapes have to be changed. Therefore, the trial stays adjourned until half past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask Mr. Koumjian, please, to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the usher could just move the ELMO back a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that Mr. Didovic in Kozarac also was speaking to a Mr. Medunjanin. Is it correct that that was Becir Medunjanin, who was a school teacher by profession?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember from that period - I'm talking about Medunjanin - I forgot his name, but I think I know which man you're referring to. Is that the person who was the president or the secretary - I no longer remember what the official name was - of the former Secretariat for National Defence which went to the SDA after the multiparty elections. So they appointed their own man, that was him, wasn't it? The name escapes me. It's an uncommon name for me, so that's exactly the kind of name I find very difficult to recall. Osme Didovic, his name is Osme Didovic, I know that because he worked with me, the same company, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about the same individual. Were you aware that Mr. Medunjanin was a school teacher?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: They were SDA people. I'd never seen him before he was appointed. And when he was appointed, I only heard about the -- about him because of the events that were happening. But then I had no contact whatsoever with his department, his service. I didn't need to have any official contacts. I never heard from him. I never saw him. I know that the person you're talking about may have him, but I can't even remember his face. I never saw the man, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that you visited Omarska three times, and there you saw some of your colleagues from the Prijedor police station and from the state security station in Prijedor, which shared the same building with you. Did you discuss with them events taking place in Omarska and the killing of people like Mr. Becir Medunjanin and Mr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Long before the war, that's if I decide to call it "war," I mean those events, one of the basic features in my line of work is that I never asked any workmate of mine what they were doing exactly because that would cast dubious light on my reasons for asking the question. I did spend time with my workmates, yes, and long before the events, my wife was an inspector in the same public security station, but she never told me anything about her work, what she worked on on a particular day. All the time we spent together, we talked about the weather, we would talk about salaries, we would discuss sports. If, for example, I asked my best friend what happened to so and so, because in my work, I really had no reason to ask, so I would give the impression that I had a reason, a hidden agenda, a reason to ask when really there was none on my part. So it was completely superfluous. I was just doing my work, and I would always just stick to my work. I wasn't asking my colleagues questions of this kind, these young ladies helping us. And one of the ladies who were helping us here around the Tribunal asked the witness about their name. And that was really -- that seemed very unpleasant, because she was supposed to just be doing her job and not supposed to know anything more than that. And that was always my line of reasoning, and that's how I treated my colleagues, too. I was there. I met Vukacin Pesic, one of the inspectors. He asked me, you had lunch already? I haven't grabbed any lunch so far, so let's go and grab some lunch together. So we would sit in their restaurant. We would share some food, we would talk about completely different things. I didn't know what he had been doing on that day or what he would be doing the next day. So that was my own policy in my job. I never wanted to give anyone any reason to believe that I had said anything to anyone that I shouldn't have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is your answer, then, that you never discussed, or no one from your workplace ever talked to you about killings in the Omarska camp, including killings of prominent, well-known people in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: There were a number of situations where I would notice -- I could see it on my colleagues' face that, how should I put it, this person, the workmate of mine, had a burden upon his back somehow, that he was preoccupied, worried about something that was happening. But especially as concerns the two persons you were asking about, those people were not really close to me. They are a different generation, and their jobs were very far, not related to mine. So the gentleman you've just mentioned, president of municipality, Cehajic, I mean, I hardly knew him. I had no reason to ask him anything, to put him any questions. Not my own colleagues, not even common people out in the street, although I kept hearing many things about people getting killed when I talked to people in the street. But you know, stuff I heard from common folks, it was, you know, unimportant. Some people talked about people getting killed, and then I heard that some people had been killed, but then I would see these very same people somewhere about town later on. So I don't know how reliable the whole thing was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that you went to Keraterm one time. Do you remember the month that you visited the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, not even roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I can't. I remember the image, the -- what I saw there, but I didn't see any of the inmates at all because I just didn't go that far into the facility. And those who had occasion to learn what the facility looked like know what I'm talking about. There are halls there with industrial -- with machines used for industrial production, and then there were some offices for administration. And that's where the inspectors were, that's where the phone was and that's where I was, too. There was a special entrance to that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You indicated that the staff appeared to you to be getting ready for a visit of internationals. And I gather that you recall hearing something about some foreigners who might be visiting that day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. A man told me, I think it was Zivko Jovic, who was an inspector, he said we have visitors today, so hurry up. I don't want to loiter about. They are coming. So I did my job and I left. And I noticed that they had this attitude as though they were expecting visitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. It would be correct that it was visitors, not necessarily internationals, but some type of delegation, some kind of prominent persons were expected to visit, according to the information you had?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was coming, but throughout that period, I know that it was either foreign journalists or humanitarian organisations with white UN vehicles. That's what I often saw, so I should suppose that they were expecting humanitarian organisation or maybe a delegation from several humanitarian organisations, journalists, perhaps. But I don't remember any military units. I think those were journalists, humanitarian aid workers, that sort of thing. But no one told me explicitly, so I just assumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you, and if you don't know the answer, you can tell me; isn't it true that Keraterm was closed before, in fact, the day that the foreign journalists were coming to Prijedor? The Keraterm camp was closed, and there were no international visits to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I didn't go there officially for my work, and there's no way for me to know that. Now, I don't have any information on this that I may have received through friends and acquaintances. I only know about that day, I was told that someone was arriving. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Zupljanin coming back in the summer of 1992 with Radoslav Brdjanin to visit Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about that visit. I only know about the day I told you about, the 9th of April, that he came and that he was not able to take the main road back, the Prijedor/Banja Luka main road. He had to pass through Kozarac, and then on through Bosanska Dubica and Bosanska Gradiska. I think that's, the distance is between 110 and 120 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mr. Drljaca was replaced in January of 1993 - if you don't know the dates, just tell us - and then eventually came back to Prijedor near the end of the war as the chief of police again?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: One thing is for sure; I don't remember the date. But I know that Drljaca was my chief only for a very short time. I went on sick leave in March 1994. He may have been in that position for three, four, or five months, but it may have been around that time but I really can't tell you the date. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When did you come back to work in the Prijedor Police Station after your sick leave?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Nearly four years. And the operation, I was operated in July 1994. The operation was a serious one. It was an eye operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you came back sometime in 1998, would that be correct, after the arrest of Mr. Drljaca -- arrest or attempted arrest of Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Drljaca was never my superior again. Formally and legally, yes, but he wasn't giving me any tasks because while he was there, I was on sick leave. So briefly, when I came back, Ranko Mijic was my supervisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was the chief of police when you came back?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Ranko Mijic, who, up to that point, used to be the chief of the crime squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did he take over, according to the information you had, from Simo Drljaca after Mr. Drljaca was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that wasn't when Simo Drljaca was killed. I think first he was removed - I don't know the reason - and he was still around but he was not working there. I think he was only killed at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Before I move on, just one brief question, I hope. You had a lot of experience during the communist period of time. Was it common during that period of time that when local leaders were removed, they were often given some type of soft landing and brought to the ministry or to the capital with another job?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. That was always the case in our country. There's a lot of bribery and corruption, and many of those who should have been punished -- for example, a police officer makes a mistake, he should be suspended from active service, but then this is taken with a lot of latitude, you know, so the police officer is allowed to retire, and sometimes pensions used to be higher than the actual salaries, so this police officer would be given more money than before, and quit work. So that used to be the case. This was a false kind of humanitarian treatment. And this applied to all the different levels, you know. There was a lot of bribery, a lot of corruption. So there was favoritism, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You've kind of introduced my next subject or my next question. Sir, during 1992, specifically between the takeover and the end of September, were you aware of any efforts to investigate or arrest Serbian police or army officers for crimes against Muslims or Croats in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please just try to rephrase your question, but make it a bit shorter if you can, because it's slightly too long and slightly too complicated. I'm afraid I might get the answer wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sure. Did you ever hear of any police or army, Serbian police or Serbian army, being arrested for killing Muslims or Croats in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: For example, our own forces, one person who was arrested, and I think he's here now in detention, Zoran Zigic. He was one of those. I didn't personally witness this, but the things I heard were so convincing that I think, yes, he had been killing people. So he was arrested, and then I don't know what charges were pressed against him in Banja Luka, but I know that he was in prison there. I don't know what the actual indictment was. He was in prison in Banja Luka. I know this because once I was on my way back from Banja Luka in my private vehicle, I was stopped at a checkpoint, and a police officer asked me to take with me a woman and two children. It was very cold. And then this woman told me that she was Zoran Zigic's wife and that she had gone to Banja Luka to visit him in prison. I can't remember if it was before or after Dayton, but it was about that time. And there was - what's his name? He was killing people in Trnopolje. He was also in prison. I can't remember what his name was. So I hear things from people, but officially, it's not part of my job, and I'm not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, let me ask this question -- if you don't know the answer, you can tell us -- isn't it correct that Mr. Zigic was arrested for killing a Serb girl and that arrest did not take place during the period between April and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, I really don't know what the counts against him were, what the indictment was, why he was being investigated. I have no idea what it was about. But I know that he had been killing people, and I know that he was in prison. Why officially, I really don't know, whether for the murder of that girl or for everyone he had killed. But you can check this with the Banja Luka Court, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, it was common knowledge in Prijedor that in July, there was a massacre at the Keraterm camp. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that it had happened. That's what I heard. I didn't witness anything, nor did I go there at this time. Who I heard it from, I don't remember. But the way people talked about those things -- you know, at work, no one talked about this. Everyone just sort of kept silent, but there was a general sense of horror. And then whenever someone brought the subject up, they would just say, "Yeah, it happened," and then people would just be very worried, concerned. No one was enthusiastic about this. I heard so, and I believe that these things indeed had happened, but how it all happened, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember in the summer of 1992, there were lines of women waiting outside the police station in Prijedor in the morning hours?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: During the whole day, from the early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could we briefly have that map of the town put back on the ELMO, please. Sorry, the number is...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, if the area is depicted on this diagram, can you show us where the women would line up.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, if I may, you're talking about people leaving Prijedor, and then coming for their documents? Is that what you're asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm specifically talking about the lines of women, and you can explain the purpose that they were there for. But the lines that you saw that you just referred to that were there all day, can you show us where they were.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was like this. This here is the police building. This is the main entrance. And this entrance here, this is a green area. This area here is surfaced, and it's perhaps between 7 and 8 metres wide. And here's the pavement. It's about 4 metres wide. Here you can see the trees, and here there was grass. A grass area. The length, so the line was here. It started here. Then down the pavement, and it was quite long in the morning. And then it grew longer and longer. And then up to here, there were poplar trees here in this place. So this is the museum building. I would say the line stretched as far as the museum building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And for the record, I'll try to describe what the -- how the witness pointed to the line. He indicated a line going first perpendicular from the SUP building, and then going out to the pavement, and then, looking at the diagram, then going to the left until the museum. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Just here where you said perpendicular, this is a very narrow patch here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you're referring to the short part of the line going perpendicular to the building, and then the line went parallel to the building. Sir, can you tell us about the intervention squad. Who commanded the intervention squad in Prijedor in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This intervention squad, we used to have drills of the reserve police forces in peacetime. And I knew the drills and the units very well. We didn't have any kind of intervention squad or platoon. And then suddenly this intervention squad turned up, it was just there suddenly. Who brought them there, who organised them, I haven't managed to understand this to this very day. But yes, they were there. They didn't have any sort of military hierarchy so you could tell who the commander was, and the soldiers lined up. They were more of a jumble really, and in motion when they were there, but sometimes only part of them was there. So I could have attempted to conclude that's the man, but then I may have been wrong. If they had a proper military unit and the commander came to meetings, the commander of this intervention squad, this never happened. I never knew the commander the way I knew the commander of the police station or the commander of the crime squad. But he was not officially part of any larger unit. But I did not know that they were part of any larger unit officially, so there was no way for me to know their commander. It still seems like an unofficial group to me. Who brought them there? Who was the commander? I'm afraid I might go wrong if I say anything. Everything would be just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that they would bring detained persons to the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you want to add something? I want to move on to another topic. But if you would like to add something --

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, just briefly, if I may add: A lot of work was done by professional police officers and professional inspectors. The whole behaviour and the whole work was very much like it had been before the war. So every person suspected of having committed a crime or a violation of any of the laws would be brought in. And then the investigating judge would give a signal for the investigation to be stopped or to go ahead. But at this time, you had a huge number of such people, and the room became very small for all the suspects. It would have taken an enormous amount of investigating judges to deal with all of them. So some of them were dealt with in a regular way and some of them were dealt with poorly in terms of procedure. So it's difficult to know, because there were many people coming in and very few people to process them. So I think that's what the poor quality of work was due to, and that's why other things happened later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, I'd like to move on to another subject. And I request, if there's no objection from anyone, to do it in private session just for the protection of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the setting up of the Omarska investigation centre, there was a station of the police Omarska. It existed even before I joined the police. And there was a radio, a fixed radio station, so not a mobile radio station, so a radio set in the room, and it also had a direct telephone line. Actually, it had two telephones; there was a public PTT connection, and there was our internal police line. And that was in the peacetime. When these unrests started, somebody, I don't know who, damaged -- I believe that there is about 20 kilometres between Prijedor and Omarska, so somebody damaged the telephone line, and for a while, we were without a telephone connection, so the only thing we used was the radio connection. When the collection centre Omarska was set up, actually, it was the first time when I heard about that, it was in the late afternoon, about an hour before the sunset, Simo Drljaca called me and told me, asked me: "Do you have a radio set on your stock? You have to go immediately. You don't have much time. Before dark, you have to go to Omarska and mount it up there. You will find our people there and they will tell you where to mount that radio station." And that's what he told me. And I asked the technician to accompany me. We took our official car, and we took the radio set, the cable, the antenna, and the whole set. We went there. I don't remember whom I found there, but whoever I found there, I knew all of them. They were all our policemen. And then they told me: "Put it there. Go upstairs and go to the first office on the right-hand side." It may have been the second right, but it certainly isn't the fifth on the right. So immediately on the right, they told me put it there, and the two of us mounted the radio station there in that place that they indicated to us. Later on, in order to establish a telephone line, I don't know how much longer after that, I engaged some postal workers who repaired their cable, the Omarska/Prijedor cable, telephone line, that is, and then they established the telephone line. And they gave the Omarska camp yet another number for the telephone. But that was much later, and I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there also a telegram line between Omarska and Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the connection between the Prijedor police office and Keraterm? Was it also necessary to set up a similar connection as you just told us?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't have a radio connection to put it there. And for practical reasons, it was not possible because it is easy to listen in to. And again, there was a town, so there were a lot more lines. It was easy to set up a connection between us and the postal building. And that's -- postal office building. That's why we established a telephone line, and I believe that up to the very end, nothing else was set up there but just that one telephone line. But they could use the mobile radio sets, the ones such as used by the policemen, by the policemen who do the patrols. That's what they used. But there was no affixed radio -- no fixed radio station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have a similar connection from Prijedor Police Station to Ljubija football stadium?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The Ljubija stadium, I don't know what you mean when you say. Why the stadium? Maybe there is a problem with the interpretation. What would we have to do with the football stadium? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe it was a separate unit, but the question would be, first, were there colleagues of yours stationed at Ljubija football stadium?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: These are the -- I know that we had a connection that we had inherited from the times before that, and that was the telephone connection and the radio connection in the facility or in the building of the police station in Ljubija. And later on, I know that some of our colleagues, Muslim colleagues, had taken that and kept it for a while, and then the others took that over. I don't remember the dates for any of these events. And I don't have any information that would put this stadium into the context of my knowledge. So I don't have any knowledge whether anybody was there, whether they were or whether they were not. I only know that there was no other connection but that one with the police station in Ljubija, that is, in the building of the police station in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clear answer. We learned that in the evening of the 29th of April, 1992, you were engaged in filling out some documents in order to prepare new IDs.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned already several names, and you told us that for this reason, you were not -- it was not possible for you to have an overview of what happened in the entire building. But may I ask you, in this room or on another occasion in Cirkin Polje at that evening, did you meet one of the following persons: Dusan Baltic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know this person. He didn't work in the SUP. Dusan Baltic, he may have been there, but that is a person I don't know and the name doesn't ring a bell. I'm sure that he was not a professional working in the SUP. I know all the colleagues there except for the younger ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Nada Markovska.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I know her well. She is a typist. She works in the crime prevention police. I didn't notice her. She may have been there, but I didn't see her. I didn't move about a lot. But it seems to me that there were no women there. I don't remember seeing any woman there on that evening. She may have been there, but I don't remember a single woman there, that is, of our employees. There were certainly none in the room where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it doesn't make sense to ask you whether you met Madam Nada Balaban?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Balaban, Mrs. Balaban; do you mean the English teacher? Balaban, Mrs. Balaban, she is a teacher of English. I'm not sure if that's the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A person working sometimes - we'll learn about this - as interpreter and, yes, maybe you're more acquainted with the name Nadja.

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Nada. I know this lady because she gave English lessons in the same kindergarten that my son went to, so that's the only reason I remember her. That was before the war. Excuse me, I never met her personally. Not in our section. I did see a tape from a German TV station. She was interpreting and Simo Drljaca and some foreign people, foreign delegation, were standing there, and she was acting as their interpreter. I saw this footage filmed, but I never witnessed this myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, the last name, did you meet there in Cirkin Polje Mr. Milovan Dragic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Milovan Dragic, if you mean Dragic, believe it or not, I met this person here at The Hague. We met here. That's the first time I saw the person, and he told me what his name was. And it was slightly unpleasant, because he knew me and I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this, once again, extremely concrete answer. But to come back to this evening of the 29th of April, I understood that you worked in one single room. What I did not understand, maybe I didn't take care enough, could you assist us: You spoke about a meeting of about 500 people. Was it at the same time, was it previous to your working in this single room? Was it later? And where did it happen; inside the building, outside the building?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did say this. I may have not been very clear. I'll try to put this very briefly. The meeting with 500 people that I talked about, that was in our meeting hall that -- when I talked about the detention room, you go through the courtyard, and on the opposite side of the courtyard that's where the meeting hall was. And the meeting was over at about half past 3.00 in the evening. I went home. They gave me a call around 8.00 in the afternoon, and then I was on my way to Cirkin Polje. It's about 4 kilometres. That would have been half past 8.00 or 9.00. It was already dark. And then due to low electricity levels in that area, the light, the street lighting wasn't very good. But the facility itself has many small rooms. And now I was in one of those rooms. And there were people milling around all the rooms and around the facility, too. Around the building outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Because we have to be extremely brief now due to time concerns, may I ask who chaired this meeting of these 500 people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat this. From left to right, sitting there, Muhamed or Muharem Cehajic. So he was there for sure. President of municipality and secondary school teacher. So I'm looking from left to right from my position. Mirza Mujadzic, head of the SDA or president of the SDA. In the middle, the chief of the station, Hasan Talundzic. Next to him, Fikret, then commander of the traffic police. And the last person to the right, Simo Miskovic. And then an empty space, and there was a rostrum there, and Radovan Krkan was standing there and he was keeping the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this precise answer. This really gives us the impression of what happened there. The final question would be one related to Document D6B-1, this very urgent telegram. Is it correct that this meant that when it was very urgent, maybe it had to be -- one had to work on this within 4 hours, or urgent 8 hours, correct? It was linked to a certain time limit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: "Very urgent" does not refer to the actions that you've just referred to. This is 8.00, or 8 hours. And that's only to check if a certain citizen was to be processed urgently or not. An operational activity would be marked as DX, and that had to be dealt with within two hours. And even more urgent matters would have had to be dealt with faster. "Very urgent" is state concern. That's what they usually refer to. And it had to be dispatched with extreme urgency, and by any means available, to the addressee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So didn't you identify the exact hour and even minute when such a document arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't memorise, but the minute and the hour have to be there in the records kept by Mirsad Sahuric and the records he handed over to the chief. So he must have recorded this. Now where is this book of records I really don't know. They are usually kept for a time period of five years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have actually one or two questions. Please, can you tell us, when did you receive the order to go to the Cirkin Polje, and from whom?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I already said this. I'm going to repeat it for you now. All tasks, all calls, everything else outside my working hours, which means when I was not physically in the police building, ever since I first started working for the police, the usual way to go about this was that my superior would always tell my duty operations officer, and they had three shifts around the clock. And as I was the head of that particular section, even if I just went over to see a friend for a coffee, I was supposed to let them know where they could find me. And every call outside my working hours -- and there were many such calls, equipment would get out of order, and then there would be some extraordinary tasks, and this belonged to the same category of events. So they called me. You know, I would receive at least three or four calls like that every single week, and then for a number of years, and it's very difficult for me to remember who exactly it was who called me on that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What sort of meeting was taking place in Cirkin Polje and how long did you stay in Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILOS JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was not a standard meeting with us sitting there and someone giving a talk. People were assembling, were gathering. Those who were active in our service, some of the leaders, department heads, mostly -- I can't say I don't know anything about that, because I was there. But I can be in a room far from there and I'm just writing, so I don't see anything but hear something. According to the best of my knowledge, what I remember now, there were five groups, each containing 20 persons. Now, whether those were the reserve forces or -- I think there were a number of military there. There may have been many of them, I didn't notice, but there were all sorts of uniforms. Not everyone had blue uniforms. So sometimes you couldn't tell whether a person was a military or a police member. Anyway, there were five groups, each containing 20 people, as far as I know, and each of the groups was led by one person, not -- with no particular striking feature so that I could remember them. I'm talking about group leaders. And they went there with the task of taking over power. As far as I know, one group was for the municipality. One group was for the SUP building. One group was headed for the court. Five groups, and I think one group was supposed to go to the bank, and the last group was supposed to take the post office. So once they had taken over all these facilities, they let us know. They came to the SUP building and it was about 7.00 in the evening. And Muslims were coming to work, so whoever accepted work in that service, because initially some of the Muslims did accept to stay, such people stayed. And those who refused to go on, they just take the official weapon off the person, as well as the official ID. But those who opted to stay on, they would just sign and they would stay. So a number of Muslims did accept at the beginning, but then they were pressed by their fellow Muslims to leave their jobs, so then they would start gradually leaving. A Muslim communications officer I referred to, Sahuric, he stayed on for a month or two after that. And then he left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any further questions by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for trying to interrupt Judge Vassylenko, but the witness said on page 120, line 8, "Whenever my superiors or somebody else called me," and it's entered only as "When my superior called me." It's not only superior, because superiors changed that night. So it might be somebody else. And the witness can clarify this, if you need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's good. I can't see any further questions. Then, it's for me to thank you for coming once again to this Tribunal and to enlighten us on that what you experienced in 1992. And I wish you a safe trip home to your home country and your home town. Thank you very much for your assistance. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: at 4.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday the 21st day of January, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
